entries.23f77f9a57e35d72976c7e86c59864900872dce6: <div sID="gen21559" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Matt.6" sID="Matt.6"/> <div eID="gen21559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21560" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21561" type="x-p"/> Christ having, in the former chapter, armed his disciples against the corrupt doctrines and opinions of the scribes and Pharisees, especially in their expositions of the law (that was called their leaven, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.12">ch. xvi. 12</reference>), comes in this chapter to warn them against their corrupt practices, against the two sins which, though in their doctrine they did not justify, yet in their conversation they were notoriously guilty of, and so as even to recommend them to their admirers: these were hypocrisy and worldly-mindedness, sins which, of all others, the professors of religion need most to guard against, as sins that most easily beset those who have escaped the grosser pollutions that are in the world through lust, and which are therefore highly dangerous. We are here cautioned, I. Against hypocrisy; we must not be as the hypocrites are, nor do as the hypocrites do. 1. In the giving of alms, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.1-Matt.6.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. 2. In prayer, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.5-Matt.6.8">ver. 5-8</reference>. We are here taught what to pray for, and how to pray (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.9-Matt.6.13">ver. 9-13</reference>); and to forgive in prayer, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.14-Matt.6.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>. 3. In fasting, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.16-Matt.6.18">ver. 16-18</reference>. II. Against worldly-mindedness, 1. In our choice, which is the destroying sin of hypocrites, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.19-Matt.6.24">ver. 19-24</reference>. 2. In our cares, which is the disquieting sin of many good Christians, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.25-Matt.6.34">ver. 25-34</reference>.
entries.c058a83375aeaad227f2f49d6fee3b0a8fc03317: <div eID="gen21561" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21560" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21562" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven. <hi type="super">2</hi> Therefore when thou doest <hi type="italic">thine</hi> alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward. <hi type="super">3</hi> But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: <hi type="super">4</hi> That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly. <div eID="gen21562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21563" type="x-p"/> As we must do better than the scribes and Pharisees in avoiding heart-sins, heart-adultery, and heart-murder, so likewise in maintaining and keeping up heart-religion, doing what we do from an inward, vital principle, that we may be approved of God, not that we may be applauded of men; that is, we must watch against hypocrisy, which was the leaven of the Pharisees, as well as against their doctrine, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.1">Luke xii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Almsgiving, prayer,</hi> and <hi type="italic">fasting,</hi> are three great Christian duties—the three foundations of the law, say the Arabians: by them we do homage and service to God with our three principal interests; by <hi type="italic">prayer</hi> with our <hi type="italic">souls,</hi> by <hi type="italic">fasting</hi> with our <hi type="italic">bodies,</hi> by <hi type="italic">alms-giving</hi> with our <hi type="italic">estates.</hi> Thus we must not only <hi type="italic">depart from evil,</hi> but <hi type="italic">do good,</hi> and do it well, and so <hi type="italic">dwell for evermore.</hi> <div eID="gen21563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21564" type="x-p"/> Now in these verses we are cautioned against hypocrisy in giving alms. <hi type="italic">Take heed</hi> of it. Our being bid to <hi type="italic">take heed</hi> of it intimates that it is sin. 1. We are in <hi type="italic">great danger of;</hi> it is a subtle sin; vain-glory insinuates itself into what we do ere we are aware. The disciples would be tempted to it by the power they had to do many wondrous works, and their living with some that admired them and others that despised them, both which are temptations to covet to make a fair show in the flesh. 2. It is a sin we are <hi type="italic">in great danger by.</hi> Take heed of hypocrisy, for if it reign in you, it will ruin you. It is the dead fly that spoils the whole box of precious ointment. <div eID="gen21564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21565" type="x-p"/> Two things are here supposed, <div eID="gen21565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21566" type="x-p"/> I. The <hi type="italic">giving of alms</hi> is a great duty, and a duty which all the disciples of Christ, according to their ability, must abound in. It is prescribed by the law of nature and of Moses, and great stress is laid upon it by the prophets. Divers ancient copies here for <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ten eleemosynen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">your alms,</hi> read <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ten dikaiosynen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">your righteousness,</hi> for <hi type="italic">alms</hi> are <hi type="italic">righteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">Ps. cxii. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.10.2">Prov. x. 2</reference>. The Jews called the <hi type="italic">poor's box</hi> the <hi type="italic">box of righteousness.</hi> That which is given to the poor is said to be their due, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.27">Prov. iii. 27</reference>. The duty is not the less necessary and excellent for its being abused by hypocrites to serve their pride. If superstitious papists have placed a merit in works of charity, that will not be an excuse for covetous protestants that are barren in such good works. It is true, our alms-deeds do not deserve heaven; but it is as true that we cannot go to heaven without them. It is <hi type="italic">pure religion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.27">Jam. i. 27</reference>), and will be the test at the great day; Christ here takes it for granted that his disciples <hi type="italic">give alms,</hi> nor will he own those that do not. <div eID="gen21566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21567" type="x-p"/> II. That it is such a duty as has a great reward attending it, which is lost if it be done in hypocrisy. It is sometimes rewarded in temporal things with <hi type="italic">plenty</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.24-Prov.11.25">Prov. xi. 24, 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.17">xix. 17</reference>); <hi type="italic">security from want</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.28.27 ">Prov. xxviii. 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.21-Ps.37.25">Ps. xxxvii. 21, 25</reference>); <hi type="italic">succour in distress</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.1-Ps.41.2">Ps. xli. 1, 2</reference>); <hi type="italic">honour and a good</hi> name, which follow those most that least covet them, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">Ps. cxii. 9</reference>. However, it shall be recompensed in the resurrection of the just (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.14">Luke xiv. 14</reference>), in <hi type="italic">eternal riches.</hi> <div eID="gen21567" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen21568"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21569"/><hi type="italic">Quas dederis, solas semper habebis, opes.</hi><l eID="gen21569" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21570"/><hi type="italic">The riches you impart form the only wealth you</hi><l eID="gen21570" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21571"/><hi type="italic">will always retain.</hi> Martial.<l eID="gen21571" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen21568"/> <div sID="gen21572" type="x-p"/> This being supposed, observe now, <div eID="gen21572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21573" type="x-p"/> 1. What was the <hi type="italic">practice of the hypocrites</hi> about this duty. They did it indeed, but not from any principle of obedience to God, or love to man, but in pride and vain-glory; not in compassion to the poor, but purely for ostentation, that they might be extolled as good men, and so might gain an interest in the esteem of the people, with which they knew how to serve their own turn, and to get a great deal more than they gave. Pursuant to this intention, they chose to give their alms <hi type="italic">in the synagogues, and in the streets,</hi> where there was the greatest concourse of people to observe them, who applauded their liberality because they shared in it, but were so ignorant as not to discern their abominable pride. Probably they had collections for the poor in the synagogues, and the common beggars haunted the streets and highways, and upon these public occasions they chose to give their alms. Not that it is unlawful to give alms <hi type="italic">when men see us;</hi> we may do it; but not <hi type="italic">that men may see us;</hi> we should rather choose those objects of charity that are less observed. The hypocrites, if they gave alms to their own houses, <hi type="italic">sounded a trumpet,</hi> under pretence of calling the poor together to be served, but really to proclaim their charity, and to have that taken notice of and made the subject of discourse. <div eID="gen21573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21574" type="x-p"/> Now the doom that Christ passes upon this is very observable; <hi type="italic">Verily I say unto you, they have their reward.</hi> At first view this seems a promise—If they have their reward they have enough, but two words in it make it a threatening. <div eID="gen21574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21575" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is a reward, but it is <hi type="italic">their</hi> reward; not the reward which God promises to them that do good, but the reward which they promise themselves, and a poor reward it is; they did it to be <hi type="italic">seen of men,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">are</hi> seen of men; they <hi type="italic">chose their own delusions</hi> with which they cheated themselves, and they shall have what they chose. Carnal professors stipulate with God for preferment, honour, wealth, and they shall have their bellies filled with those things (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>); but let them expect no more; these are their consolation (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.24">Luke vi. 24</reference>), their good things (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Luke xvi. 25</reference>), and they shall be put off with these. "<hi type="italic">Didst thou not agree with me for a penny?</hi> It is the bargain that thou art likely to abide by." <div eID="gen21575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21576" type="x-p"/> (2.) It is a reward, but it is a <hi type="italic">present reward,</hi> they <hi type="italic">have</hi> it; and there is none reserved for them in the future state. They now have all that they are likely to have from God; they have their reward here, and have none to hope for hereafter. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Apechousi ton misthon</hi></hi>. It signifies a <hi type="italic">receipt in full.</hi> What rewards the godly have in this life are but <hi type="italic">in part of payment;</hi> there is more behind, much more; but hypocrites have their <hi type="italic">all</hi> in this world, so shall their doom be; themselves have decided it. The world is but for <hi type="italic">provision</hi> to the saints, it is their spending-money; but it is <hi type="italic">pay</hi> to hypocrites, it is their portion. <div eID="gen21576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21577" type="x-p"/> 2. What is the <hi type="italic">precept of our Lord Jesus</hi> about it, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.3-Matt.6.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. He that was himself such an example of humility, pressed it upon his disciples, as absolutely necessary to the acceptance of their performances. "<hi type="italic">Let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth</hi> when thou givest alms." Perhaps this alludes to the placing of the Corban, the poor man's box, or the chest into which they cast their free-will offerings, <hi type="italic">on the right hand</hi> of the passage into the temple; so that they put their gifts into it with the <hi type="italic">right-hand.</hi> Or the giving of alms with the <hi type="italic">right hand,</hi> intimates readiness to it and resolution in it; do it dexterously, not awkwardly nor with a sinister intention. The <hi type="italic">right hand</hi> may be used in helping the poor, lifting them up, writing for them, dressing their sores, and other ways besides giving to them; but, "whatever kindness thy right hand doeth to the poor, <hi type="italic">let not thy left hand know it:</hi> conceal it as much as possible; industriously keep it private. Do it because it is a good work, not because it will give thee a good name." <hi type="italic">In omnibus factis, re, non teste, moveamur—In all our actions, we should be influenced by a regard to the object, not to the observer.</hi> Cic. de Fin. It is intimated, (1.) That we must not let <hi type="italic">others</hi> know what we do; no, not those that stand <hi type="italic">at our left hand,</hi> that are very near us. Instead of acquainting them with it, keep it from them if possible; however, appear so desirous to keep it from them, as that in civility they may seem not to take notice of it, and keep it to themselves, and let it go no further. (2.) That we must not observe it too much <hi type="italic">ourselves:</hi> the left hand is a part of ourselves; we must not within ourselves take notice too much of the good we do, must not applaud and admire ourselves. Self-conceit and self-complacency, and an adoring of our own shadow, are branches of pride, as dangerous as vain-glory and ostentation before men. We find those had their good works remembered to their honour, who had themselves forgotten them: <hi type="italic">When saw we thee an hungered, or athirst?</hi> <div eID="gen21577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21578" type="x-p"/> 3. What is the <hi type="italic">promise to those who are thus sincere and humble</hi> in their alms-giving. Let <hi type="italic">thine alms be in secret,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">thy Father who seeth in secret</hi> will observe them. Note, When we take least notice of our good deeds ourselves, God takes most notice of them. As God hears the wrongs done to us when we do not hear them (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.14-Ps.38.15">Ps. xxxviii. 14, 15</reference>), so he sees the good done by us, when we do not see it. As it is a terror to hypocrites, so it is a comfort to sincere Christians, that God <hi type="italic">sees in secret.</hi> But this is not all; not only the observation and praise, but the recompence is of God, <hi type="italic">himself shall reward thee openly.</hi> Note, They who in their alms-giving study to approve themselves to God, only turn themselves over to him as their Paymaster. The hypocrite catches at the shadow, but the upright man makes sure of the substance. Observe how emphatically it is expressed; <hi type="italic">himself shall reward,</hi> he will himself be the Rewarder, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.6">Heb. xi. 6</reference>. Let him alone to make it up in kind or kindness; nay, he will <hi type="italic">himself be the Reward</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">Gen. xv. 1</reference>), thine <hi type="italic">exceeding great reward.</hi> He will reward thee as thy Father, not as a master who gives his servant just what he earns and no more, but as a father who gives abundantly more, and without stint, to his son that serves him. Nay, he shall reward thee <hi type="italic">openly,</hi> if not in the present day, yet in the great day; <hi type="italic">then shall every man have praise of God,</hi> open praise, thou shall be confessed <hi type="italic">before men.</hi> If the work be not open, the reward shall, and that is better.
entries.4e7ddce83239096cc4d782d003ab78a822009cea: <div eID="gen21578" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21579" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> And when thou prayest, thou shalt not be as the hypocrites <hi type="italic">are:</hi> for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward. <hi type="super">6</hi> But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly. <hi type="super">7</hi> But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen <hi type="italic">do:</hi> for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking. 8 Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him. <div eID="gen21579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21580" type="x-p"/> In <hi type="italic">prayer</hi> we have more immediately to do with God than in <hi type="italic">giving alms,</hi> and therefore are yet more concerned to be <hi type="italic">sincere,</hi> which is what we are here directed to. <hi type="italic">When thou prayest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.5">v. 5</reference>). It is taken for granted that all the disciples of Christ <hi type="italic">pray.</hi> As soon as ever Paul was converted, <hi type="italic">behold he prayeth.</hi> You may as soon find a living man that does not breathe, as a living Christian that does not pray. <hi type="italic">For this shall every one that is godly pray.</hi> If prayerless, then graceless. "<hi type="italic">Now, when thou prayest,</hi> thou shalt not be <hi type="italic">as the hypocrites are,</hi> nor do as they do," <reference osisRef="Matt.6.2">v. 2</reference>. Note, Those who would not do as the hypocrites do in their ways and actions must not be as the hypocrites are in their frame and temper. He names nobody, but it appears by <reference osisRef="Matt.23.13">ch. xxiii. 13</reference>, that by the hypocrites here he means especially the scribes and Pharisees. <div eID="gen21580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21581" type="x-p"/> Now there were two great faults they were guilty of in prayer, against each of which we are here cautioned—vain-glory (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.5-Matt.6.6">v. 5, 6</reference>); and vain repetitions, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.7-Matt.6.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. <div eID="gen21581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21582" type="x-p"/> I. We must not be <hi type="italic">proud</hi> and <hi type="italic">vain-glorious</hi> in prayer, nor aim at the praise of men. And here observe, <div eID="gen21582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21583" type="x-p"/> 1. What was the <hi type="italic">way and practice of the hypocrites.</hi> In all their exercises of devotion, it was plain, the chief thing they aimed at was to be commended by their neighbours, and thereby to make an interest for themselves. When they seemed to <hi type="italic">soar upwards</hi> in prayer (and if it be right, it is the soul's ascent toward God), yet even then their eye was <hi type="italic">downwards</hi> upon this as their <hi type="italic">prey.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen21583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21584" type="x-p"/> (1.) What the <hi type="italic">places</hi> were which they chose for their devotions; they prayed in the <hi type="italic">synagogues,</hi> which were indeed proper places for public prayer, but not for personal. They pretended hereby to do honour to the place of their assemblies, but intended to do honour to themselves. They prayed in <hi type="italic">the corners of the streets,</hi> the broad streets (so the word signifies), which were most frequented. They withdrew thither, as if they were under a pious impulse which would not admit delay, but really it was to cause themselves to be taken notice of. There, where two streets met, they were not only within view of both, but every passenger turning close upon them would observe them, and hear what they said. <div eID="gen21584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21585" type="x-p"/> (2.) The <hi type="italic">posture</hi> they used in prayer; they prayed standing; this is a lawful and proper posture for prayer (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.25">Mark xi. 25</reference>, <hi type="italic">When ye stand praying</hi>), but kneeling being the more humble and reverent gesture, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.41">Luke xxii. 41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.60">Acts vii. 60</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.14">Eph. iii. 14</reference>, their standing seemed to savour of pride and confidence in themselves (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.11">Luke xviii. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">The Pharisee stood and prayed.</hi> <div eID="gen21585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21586" type="x-p"/> (3.) Their <hi type="italic">pride</hi> in choosing these public places, which is expressed in two things: [1.] They <hi type="italic">love</hi> to pray there. They did not love prayer for its own sake, but they loved it when it gave them an opportunity of making themselves noticed. Circumstances may be such, that our good deeds must needs be done openly, so as to fall under the observation of others, and be commended by them; but the sin and danger is when we love it, and are pleased with it, because it feeds the proud humour. [2.] It is that they may be <hi type="italic">seen of men;</hi> not that God might accept them, but that men might admire and applaud them; and that they might easily get the estates of widows and orphans into their hands (who would not trust such devout, praying men?) and that, when they had them, they might devour them without being suspected (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.14">ch. xxiii. 14</reference>); and effectually carry on their public designs to enslave the people. <div eID="gen21586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21587" type="x-p"/> (4.) The <hi type="italic">product</hi> of all this, <hi type="italic">they have their reward;</hi> they have all the recompence they must ever expect from God for their service, and a poor recompence it is. What will it avail us to have the good word of our fellow-servants, if our Master do not say, <hi type="italic">Well done?</hi> But if in so great a transaction as is between us and God, when we are at prayer, we can take in so poor a consideration as the praise of men is, it is just that that should be all our reward. They did it to be <hi type="italic">seen of men,</hi> and they are so; and much good may it do them. Note, Those that would approve themselves to God by their integrity in their religion, must have no regard to the praise of men; it is not to men that we pray, nor from them that we expect an answer; they are not to be our judges, they are dust and ashes like ourselves, and therefore we must not have our eye to them: what passes between God and our own souls must be out of sight. In our synagogue-worship, we must avoid every thing that tends to make our personal devotion remarkable, as they that caused their <hi type="italic">voice to be heard on high,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.58.4">Isa. lviii. 4</reference>. Public places are not proper for private solemn prayer. <div eID="gen21587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21588" type="x-p"/> 2. What is the <hi type="italic">will of Jesus Christ</hi> in opposition to this. Humility and sincerity are the two great lessons that Christ teaches us; <hi type="italic">Thou, when thou prayest,</hi> do so and so (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.6">v. 6</reference>); <hi type="italic">thou</hi> in particular by thyself, and for thyself. Personal prayer is here supposed to be the duty and practice of all Christ's disciples. <div eID="gen21588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21589" type="x-p"/> Observe, (1.) The directions here given about it. <div eID="gen21589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21590" type="x-p"/> [1.] Instead of praying in <hi type="italic">the synagogues</hi> and in the <hi type="italic">corners of the streets, enter into thy closet,</hi> into some place of privacy and retirement. Isaac went into the field (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.63">Gen. xxiv. 63</reference>), Christ to a mountain, Peter to a housetop. No place amiss in point of ceremony, if it do but answer the end. Note, Secret prayer is to be performed in retirement, that we may be unobserved, and so may avoid ostentation; undisturbed, and so may avoid distraction; unheard, and so may use greater freedom; yet if the circumstances be such that we cannot possibly avoid being taken notice of, we must not therefore neglect the duty, lest the omission be a greater scandal than the observation of it. <div eID="gen21590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21591" type="x-p"/> [2.] Instead of doing it to be <hi type="italic">seen of men, pray to thy Father who is in secret; to me, even to me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.7.5-Zech.7.6">Zech. vii. 5, 6</reference>. The Pharisees prayed rather to men than to God; whatever was the form of their prayer, the scope of it was to beg the applause of men, and court their favours. "Well, do thou pray to God, and let that be enough for thee. Pray to him as a Father, as thy Father, ready to hear and answer, graciously inclined to pity, help, and succour thee. Pray to thy Father <hi type="italic">who is in secret.</hi>" Note, In secret prayer we must have an eye to God, as present in all places; he is there in thy closet when no one else is there; there especially nigh to thee in what thou <hi type="italic">callest upon him for.</hi> By <hi type="italic">secret</hi> prayer we give God the glory of his universal presence (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.24">Acts xvii. 24</reference>), and may take to ourselves the comfort of it. <div eID="gen21591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21592" type="x-p"/> (2.) The encouragements here given us to it. <div eID="gen21592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21593" type="x-p"/> [1.] Thy Father <hi type="italic">seeth in secret;</hi> his eye is upon thee to accept thee, when the eye of no man is upon thee to applaud thee; <hi type="italic">under the fig-tree, I saw thee,</hi> said Christ to Nathaniel, <reference osisRef="John.1.48">John i. 48</reference>. He saw Paul at prayer in such a street, at such a house, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.11">Acts ix. 11</reference>. There is not a secret, sudden breathing after God, but he observes it. <div eID="gen21593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21594" type="x-p"/> [2.] He <hi type="italic">will reward thee openly;</hi> they have their reward that do it openly, and thou shalt not lose thine for thy doing it in secret. It is called a <hi type="italic">reward,</hi> but it is <hi type="italic">of grace,</hi> not <hi type="italic">of debt;</hi> what merit can there be in begging? The reward will be open; they shall not only have it, but have it honourably: the open reward is that which hypocrites are fond of, but they have not patience to stay for it; it is that which the sincere are dead to, and they shall have it over and above. Sometimes secret prayers are rewarded openly in this world by signal answers to them, which manifests God's praying people in the consciences of their adversaries; however, at the great day there will be an open reward, when all praying people shall <hi type="italic">appear in glory</hi> with the great Intercessor. The Pharisees ha their reward <hi type="italic">before all the town,</hi> and it was a <hi type="italic">mere flash and shadow;</hi> true Christians shall have theirs <hi type="italic">before all the world,</hi> angels and men, and it shall be a <hi type="italic">weight of glory.</hi> <div eID="gen21594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21595" type="x-p"/> II. We must not <hi type="italic">use vain repetitions</hi> in prayer, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.7-Matt.6.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Though the life of prayer lies in <hi type="italic">lifting up the soul and pouring out the heart,</hi> yet there is some interest which words have in prayer, especially in joint prayer; for in that, words are necessary, and it should seem that our Saviour speaks here especially of that; for before he said, <hi type="italic">when thou prayest,</hi> he here, when <hi type="italic">ye pray;</hi> and the Lord's prayer which follows is a joint prayer, and in that, he that is the mouth of others is most tempted to an ostentation of language and expression, against which we are here warned; <hi type="italic">use not vain repetitions,</hi> either alone or with others: the Pharisees affected this, <hi type="italic">they made long prayers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.14">ch. xxiii. 14</reference>), all their care was to make them long. Now observe, <div eID="gen21595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21596" type="x-p"/> 1. What the <hi type="italic">fault</hi> is that is here reproved and condemned; it is making a mere lip-labour of the duty of prayer, the service of the tongue, when it is not the service of the soul. This is expressed here by two words, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Battologia, Polylogia</hi></hi>. (1.) <hi type="italic">Vain repetitions</hi>—tautology, battology, idle babbling over the same words again and again to no purpose, like <hi type="italic">Battus, Sub illis montibus erant, erant sub montibus illis;</hi> like that imitation of the wordiness of a fool, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.14">Eccl. x. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">A man cannot tell what shall be; and what shall be after him who can tell?</hi> which is indecent and nauseous in any discourse, much more in speaking to God. It is not all repetition in prayer that is here condemned, but vain repetitions. Christ himself prayed, saying the same words (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.44">ch. xxvi. 44</reference>), out of more than ordinary fervour and zeal, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.44">Luke xxii. 44</reference>. So Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.18-Dan.9.19">ch. ix. 18, 19</reference>. And there is a very elegant repetition of the same words, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.1-Ps.136.26">Ps. cxxxvi.</reference>. It may be of use both to express our own affections, and to excite the affections of others. But the superstitious rehearsing of a tale of words, without regard to the sense of them, as the papists saying by their beads so many Ave-Marys and Paternosters; or the barren and dry going over of the same things again and again, merely to drill out the prayer to such a length, and to make a show of affection when really there is none; these are the vain repetitions here condemned. When we would fain say much, but cannot say much to the purpose; this is displeasing to God and all wise men. (2.) <hi type="italic">Much speaking,</hi> an affectation of prolixity in prayer, either out of pride or superstition, or an opinion that God needs either to be informed or argued with by us, or out of mere folly and impertinence, because men love to <hi type="italic">hear themselves talk.</hi> Not that all long prayers are forbidden; Christ prayed all night, <reference osisRef="Luke.6.12">Luke vi. 12</reference>. Solomon's was a long prayer. There is sometimes need of long prayers when our errands and our affections are extraordinary; but merely to prolong the prayer, as if it would make it more pleasing or more prevailing with God, is that which is here condemned; it is not much <hi type="italic">praying</hi> that is condemned; no, we are bid to <hi type="italic">pray always,</hi> but much <hi type="italic">speaking;</hi> the danger of this error is when we only <hi type="italic">say</hi> our prayers, and not when we <hi type="italic">pray</hi> them. This caution is explained by that of Solomon (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.2">Eccl. v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">Let thy words be few,</hi> considerate and well weighed; <hi type="italic">take with you words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.2">Hos. xiv. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">choose out words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.9.14">Job ix. 14</reference>), and do not say every thing that comes uppermost. <div eID="gen21596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21597" type="x-p"/> 2. What reasons are given against this. <div eID="gen21597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21598" type="x-p"/> (1.) This is the way of the heathen, <hi type="italic">as the heathen do;</hi> and it ill becomes Christians to worship their God as the Gentiles worship theirs. The heathen were taught by the light of nature to worship God; but becoming vain in their imaginations concerning the object of their worship, no wonder they became so concerning the manner of it, and particularly in this instance; thinking God altogether such a one as themselves, they thought he needed many words to make him understand what was said to him, or to bring him to comply with their requests; as if he were weak and ignorant, and hard to be entreated. Thus Baal's priests were hard at it from morning till almost night with their <hi type="italic">vain repetitions;</hi> <hi type="italic">O Baal, hear us;</hi> <hi type="italic">O Baal, hear us;</hi> and vain petitions they were; but Elijah, in a grave, composed frame, with a very concise prayer, prevailed for fire from heaven first, and then water, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.26">1 Kings xviii. 26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.36">36</reference>. <hi type="italic">Lip-labour</hi> in prayer, though ever so well <hi type="italic">laboured,</hi> if that be all, is but <hi type="italic">lost labour.</hi> <div eID="gen21598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21599" type="x-p"/> (2.) "It need not be your way, <hi type="italic">for your Father</hi> in heaven <hi type="italic">knoweth what things ye have need of before ye ask him,</hi> and therefore there is no occasion for such abundance of words. It does not follow that therefore ye need not pray; for God requires you by prayer to own your need of him and dependence on him, and to please his promises; but therefore you are to open your case, and pour out your hearts before him, and then leave it with him." Consider, [1.] The God we pray to is our Father by creation, by covenant; and therefore our addresses to him should be easy, natural, and unaffected; children do not use to make long speeches to their parents when they want any thing; it is enough to say, <hi type="italic">my head, my head.</hi> Let us come to him with the disposition of children, with love, reverence, and dependence; and then they need not say many words, that are taught by the Spirit of adoption to say that one aright, <hi type="italic">Abba, Father.</hi> [2.] He is a Father that knows our case and knows our wants better than we do ourselves. <hi type="italic">He knows what things we have need of;</hi> his eyes run to and fro through the earth, to observe the necessities of his people (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2 Chron. xvi. 9</reference>), and he often gives <hi type="italic">before we call</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.24">Isa. lxv. 24</reference>), and <hi type="italic">more than we ask for</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.20">Eph. iii. 20</reference>), and if he do not give his people what they ask, it is because he knows they do not need it, and that it is not for their good; and of that he is fitter to judge for us than we for ourselves. We need not be long, nor use many words in representing our case; God knows it better than we can tell him, only he will know it <hi type="italic">from us (what will ye that I should do unto you?</hi>); and when we have told him what it is, we must refer ourselves to him, <hi type="italic">Lord, all my desire is before thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.9">Ps. xxxviii. 9</reference>. So far is God from being wrought upon by the length or language of our prayers, that the most powerful intercessions are those which are made with <hi type="italic">groanings that cannot be uttered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Rom. viii. 26</reference>. We are not to <hi type="italic">pre</hi>scribe, but <hi type="italic">sub</hi>scribe to God.
entries.6fb2d27cacea19bbcbfcf3e7a7b3c17643ace7c2: <div eID="gen21599" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21600" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. <hi type="super">10</hi> Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> in heaven. 11 Give us this day our daily bread. <hi type="super">12</hi> And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. <hi type="super">13</hi> And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen. <hi type="super">14</hi> For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: <hi type="super">15</hi> But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. <div eID="gen21600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21601" type="x-p"/> When Christ had condemned what was amiss, he directs to do better; for his are reproofs of instruction. Because we know not what to pray for as we ought, he here helps our infirmities, by putting words into our mouths; <hi type="italic">after this manner therefore pray ye,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.9">v. 9</reference>. So many were the corruptions that had crept into this duty of prayer among the Jews, that Christ saw it needful to give a new directory for prayer, to show his disciples what must ordinarily be the matter and method of their prayer, which he gives in words that may very well be used as a form; as the summary or contents of the several particulars of our prayers. Not that we are tied up to the use of this form only, or of this always, as if this were necessary to the consecrating of our other prayers; we are here bid to pray after this manner, with these words, or to this effect. That in Luke differs from this; we do not find it used by the apostles; we are not here taught to pray in the name of Christ, as we are afterward; we are here taught to pray that the kingdom might come which did come when the Spirit was poured out: yet, without doubt, it is very good to use it as a form, and it is a pledge of the communion of saints, it having been used by the church in all ages, at least (says Dr. Whitby) from the third century. It is our Lord's prayer, it is of his composing, of his appointing; it is very compendious, yet very comprehensive, in compassion to our infirmities in praying. The matter is choice and necessary, the method instructive, and the expression very concise. It has much in a little, and it is requisite that we acquaint ourselves with the sense and meaning of it, for it is used acceptably no further than it is used with understanding and without vain repetition. <div eID="gen21601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21602" type="x-p"/> The Lord's prayer (as indeed every prayer) is a letter sent from earth to heaven. Here is the inscription of the letter, the person to whom it is directed, <hi type="italic">our Father;</hi> the where, <hi type="italic">in heaven;</hi> the contents of it in several errands of request; the close, <hi type="italic">for thine is the kingdom;</hi> the seal, <hi type="italic">Amen;</hi> and if you will, the date too, <hi type="italic">this day.</hi> <div eID="gen21602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21603" type="x-p"/> Plainly thus: there are three parts of the prayer. <div eID="gen21603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21604" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">The preface, Our Father who art in heaven.</hi> Before we come to our business, there must be a solemn address to him with whom our business lies; <hi type="italic">Our Father.</hi> Intimating, that we must pray, not only alone and for ourselves, but with and for others; for we are members one of another, and are called into fellowship with each other. We are here taught <hi type="italic">to whom to pray,</hi> to God only, and not to saints and angels, for they are ignorant of us, are not to have the high honours we give in prayer, nor can give favours we expect. We are taught how to address ourselves to God, and what title to give him, that which speaks him rather beneficent than magnificent, for we are to come boldly to the throne of grace. <div eID="gen21604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21605" type="x-p"/> 1. We must address ourselves to him as <hi type="italic">our Father,</hi> and must call him so. He is a common Father to all mankind by creation, <reference osisRef="Mal.2.10">Mal. ii. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.28">Acts xvii. 28</reference>. He is in a special manner a Father to the saints, by adoption and regeneration (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.5">Eph. i. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Gal. iv. 6</reference>); and an unspeakable privilege it is. Thus we must eye him in prayer, keep up good thoughts of him, such as are encouraging and not affrighting; nothing more pleasing to God, nor pleasant to ourselves, than to call God <hi type="italic">Father.</hi> Christ in prayer mostly called God <hi type="italic">Father.</hi> If he be our Father, he will pity us under our weaknesses and infirmities (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.13">Ps. ciii. 13</reference>), will spare us (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.17">Mal. iii. 17</reference>), will make the best of our performances, though very defective, will deny us nothing that is good for us, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.11-Luke.11.13">Luke xi. 11-13</reference>. We have access with boldness to him, as to a father, and have an <hi type="italic">advocate with the Father,</hi> and the Spirit of adoption. When we come repenting of our sins, we must eye God as a Father, as the prodigal did (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.18">Luke xv. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.19">Jer. iii. 19</reference>); when we come begging for grace, and peace, and the inheritance and blessing of sons, it is an encouragement that we come to God, not as an unreconciled, avenging Judge, but as a loving, gracious, reconciled Father in Christ, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.4">Jer. iii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen21605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21606" type="x-p"/> 2. As our Father <hi type="italic">in heaven:</hi> so in heaven as to be every where else, for the heaven cannot contain him; yet so in heaven as there to manifest his glory, for it is his throne (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.19">Ps. ciii. 19</reference>), and it is to believers a throne of grace: thitherward we must direct our prayers, for Christ the Mediator is now in heaven, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.1">Heb. viii. 1</reference>. Heaven is out of sight, and a world of spirits, therefore our converse with God in prayer must be spiritual; it is on high, therefore in prayer we must be raised above the world, and lift up our hearts, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.1">Ps. v. 1</reference>. Heaven is a place of perfect purity, and we must therefore lift up pure hands, must study to sanctify his name, who is the Holy One, and dwells in that holy place, <reference osisRef="Lev.10.3">Lev. x. 3</reference>. From heaven God beholds the children of men, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.13-Ps.33.14">Ps. xxxiii. 13, 14</reference>. And we must in prayer see his eye upon us: thence he has a full and clear view of all our wants and burdens and desires, and all our infirmities. It is the firmament of his power likewise, as well as of his prospect, <reference osisRef="Ps.150.1">Ps. cl. 1</reference>. He is not only, as a Father, able to help us, able to do great things for us, more than we can ask or think; he has wherewith to supply our needs, for every good gift is from above. He is a Father, and therefore we may come to him with boldness, but a Father in heaven, and therefore we must come with reverence, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.2">Eccl. v. 2</reference>. Thus all our prayers should correspond with that which is our great aim as Christians, and that is, to be with God in heaven. God and heaven, the end of our whole conversation, must be particularly eyed in every prayer; there is the centre to which we are all tending. By prayer, we send before us thither, where we profess to be going. <div eID="gen21606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21607" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">The petitions,</hi> and those are six; the three first relating more immediately to God and his honour, the three last to our own concerns, both temporal and spiritual; as in the ten commandments, the four first teach us our duty toward God, and the last six our duty toward our neighbour. The method of this prayer teaches us to seek first the <hi type="italic">kingdom of God and his righteousness,</hi> and then to hope that <hi type="italic">other things shall be added.</hi> <div eID="gen21607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21608" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">Hallowed be thy name.</hi> It is the same word that in other places is translated <hi type="italic">sanctified.</hi> But here the old word <hi type="italic">hallowed</hi> is retained, only because people were used to it in the Lord's prayer. In these words, (1.) We give glory to God; it may be taken not as a petition, but as an adoration; as that, <hi type="italic">the Lord be magnified,</hi> or <hi type="italic">glorified,</hi> for God's holiness is the greatness and glory of all his perfections. We must begin our prayers with praising God, and it is very fit he should be first served, and that we should give glory to God, before we expect to receive mercy and grace from him. Let him have praise of his perfections, and then let us have the benefit of them. (2.) We fix our end, and it is the right end to be aimed at, and ought to be our chief and ultimate end in all our petitions, that God may be glorified; all our other requests must be in subordination to this, and in pursuance of it. "<hi type="italic">Father, glorify thyself</hi> in giving me my daily bread and pardoning my sins," &c. Since all is of him and through him, all must be to him and for him. In prayer our thoughts and affections should be carried out most to the glory of God. The Pharisees made their own name the chief end of their prayers (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.5">v. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">to be seen of men</hi>), in opposition to which we are directed to make the name of God our chief end; let all our petitions centre in this and be regulated by it. "Do so and so for me, <hi type="italic">for the glory of thy name,</hi> and as far as is for the glory of it." (3.) We desire and pray that the name of God, that is, God himself, in all that whereby he has made himself known, may be sanctified and glorified both by us and others, and especially by himself. "Father, let thy name be glorified as a Father, and a Father in heaven; glorify thy goodness and thy highness, thy majesty and mercy. <hi type="italic">Let thy name be sanctified,</hi> for it is a holy name; no matter what becomes of our polluted names, but, Lord, <hi type="italic">what wilt thou do to thy great name?</hi>" When we pray that God's name may be glorified, [1.] We make a virtue of necessity; for God will <hi type="italic">sanctify his own name,</hi> whether we desire it or not; <hi type="italic">I will be exalted among the heathen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.46.10">Ps. lxvi. 10</reference>. [2.] We ask for that which we are sure shall be granted; for when our Saviour prayed, <hi type="italic">Father glorify thy name,</hi> it was immediately answered, <hi type="italic">I have glorified it, and will glorify it again.</hi> <div eID="gen21608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21609" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">Thy kingdom come.</hi> This petition has plainly a reference to the doctrine which Christ preached at this time, which John Baptist had preached before, and which he afterwards sent his apostles out to preach—<hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven is at hand.</hi> The kingdom of your Father who is in heaven, the kingdom of the Messiah, this is at hand, pray that it may come. Note, We should turn the word we hear into prayer, our hearts should echo to it; does Christ promise, <hi type="italic">surely I come quickly?</hi> our hearts should answer, <hi type="italic">Even so, come.</hi> Ministers should pray over the word: when they preach, <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God is at hand,</hi> they should pray, <hi type="italic">Father, thy kingdom come.</hi> What God has promised we must pray for; for promises are given, not to supersede, but to quicken and encourage prayer; and when the accomplishment of a promise is near and at the door, when the kingdom of heaven is at hand, we should then pray for it the more earnestly; <hi type="italic">thy kingdom come;</hi> as Daniel set his face to pray for the deliverance of Israel, when he understood that the time of it was at hand, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.2">Dan. ix. 2</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Luke.19.11">Luke xix. 11</reference>. It was the Jews' daily prayer to God, <hi type="italic">Let him make his kingdom reign, let his redemption flourish, and let his Messiah come and deliver his people.</hi> Dr. Whitby, <hi type="italic">ex Vitringa.</hi> "<hi type="italic">Let thy kingdom come,</hi> let the gospel be preached to all and embraced by all; let all be brought to subscribe to the record God has given in his word concerning his Son, and to embrace him as their Saviour and Sovereign. Let the bounds of the gospel-church be enlarged, the kingdom of the world be made Christ's kingdom, and all men become subjects to it, and live as becomes their character." <div eID="gen21609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21610" type="x-p"/> 3. <hi type="italic">Thy will be done in earth as it is in heaven.</hi> We pray that God's kingdom being come, we and others may be brought into obedience to all the laws and ordinances of it. By this let it appear that Christ's kingdom is come, <hi type="italic">let God's will be done;</hi> and by this let is appear that it is come as a <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven,</hi> let it introduce a <hi type="italic">heaven upon earth.</hi> We make Christ but a titular Prince, if we call him King, and do not do his will: having prayed that he may rule us, we pray that we may in every thing be ruled by him. Observe, (1.) The thing prayed for, <hi type="italic">thy will be done;</hi> "Lord, do what thou pleasest with me and mine; <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.18">1 Sam. iii. 18</reference>. I refer myself to thee, and am well satisfied that all thy counsel concerning me should be performed." In this sense Christ prayed, <hi type="italic">not my will, but thine be done.</hi> "Enable me to do what is pleasing to thee; give me that grace that is necessary to the right knowledge of thy will, and an acceptable obedience to it. Let thy will be done conscientiously by me and others, not our own will, the will of the flesh, or the mind, not the will of men (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.2">1 Pet. iv. 2</reference>), much less Satan's will (<reference osisRef="John.8.44">John viii. 44</reference>), that we may neither displease God in any thing we do (<hi type="italic">ut nihil nostrum displiceat Deo</hi>), nor be displeased at any thing God does" (<hi type="italic">ut nihil Dei displiceat nobis</hi>). (2.) The pattern of it, that it might be <hi type="italic">done on earth,</hi> in this place of our trial and probation (where our work must be done, or it never will be done), <hi type="italic">as it is done in heaven,</hi> that place of rest and joy. We pray that earth may be made more like heaven by the observance of God's will (this earth, which, through the prevalency of Satan's will, has become so near akin to hell), and that saints may be made more like the holy angels in their devotion and obedience. We are <hi type="italic">on earth,</hi> blessed be God, not yet <hi type="italic">under the earth;</hi> we pray for the <hi type="italic">living</hi> only, not for <hi type="italic">the dead that have gone down into silence.</hi> <div eID="gen21610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21611" type="x-p"/> 4. <hi type="italic">Give us this day our daily bread.</hi> Because our natural being is necessary to our spiritual well-being in this world, therefore, after the things of God's glory, kingdom, and will, we pray for the necessary supports and comforts of this present life, which are the gifts of God, and must be asked of him, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Ton arton epiousion</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Bread for the day approaching,</hi> for all the remainder of our lives. <hi type="italic">Bread for the time to come, or bread for our being and subsistence,</hi> that which is agreeable to our condition in the world (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.8">Prov. xxx. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">food convenient for us</hi> and our families, according to our rank and station. <div eID="gen21611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21612" type="x-p"/> Every word here has a lesson in it: (1.) We ask for <hi type="italic">bread;</hi> that teaches us sobriety and temperance; we ask for <hi type="italic">bread,</hi> not dainties, not superfluities; that which is wholesome, though it be not nice. (2.) We ask for <hi type="italic">our</hi> bread; that teaches us honesty and industry: we do not ask for the bread out of other people's mouths, not the <hi type="italic">bread of deceit</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.20.17">Prov. xx. 17</reference>), not the <hi type="italic">bread of idleness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.27">Prov. xxxi. 27</reference>), but the bread honestly gotten. (3.) We ask for our <hi type="italic">daily</hi> bread; which teaches us not to <hi type="italic">take thought for the morrow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.34">v. 34</reference>), but constantly to depend upon divine Providence, as those that live from hand to mouth. (4.) We beg of God to <hi type="italic">give</hi> it us, not sell it us, nor lend it us, but <hi type="italic">give</hi> it. The greatest of men must be beholden to the mercy of God for their <hi type="italic">daily bread,</hi> (5.) We pray, "Give it to <hi type="italic">us;</hi> not to me only, but to others in common with me." This teaches us charity, and a compassionate concern for the poor and needy. It intimates also, that we ought to pray with our families; we and our households eat together, and therefore ought to pray together. (6.) We pray that God would give us <hi type="italic">this day;</hi> which teaches us to renew the desire of our souls toward God, as the wants of our bodies are renewed; as duly as the day comes, we must pray to our heavenly Father, and reckon we could as well go a day without meat, as without prayer. <div eID="gen21612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21613" type="x-p"/> 5. <hi type="italic">And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors,</hi> This is connected with the former; and <hi type="italic">forgive,</hi> intimating, that unless our sins be pardoned, we can have no comfort in life, or the supports of it. <hi type="italic">Our daily bread</hi> does but feed us <hi type="italic">as lambs for the slaughter,</hi> if our sins be not pardoned. It intimates, likewise, that we must pray for daily <hi type="italic">pardon,</hi> as duly as we pray for daily <hi type="italic">bread.</hi> <hi type="italic">He that is washed, needeth to wash his feet.</hi> Here we have, <div eID="gen21613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21614" type="x-p"/> (1.) A petition; <hi type="italic">Father in heaven forgive us our debts,</hi> our debts to thee. Note, [1.] Our sins are our debts; there is a debt of duty, which, as creatures, we owe to our Creator; we do not pray to be discharged from that, but upon the non-payment of that there arises a debt of punishment; in default of obedience to the will of God, we become obnoxious <hi type="italic">to the wrath of God;</hi> and for not observing the precept of the law, we stand obliged to the penalty. A debtor is liable to process, so are we; a malefactor is a debtor to the law, so are we. [2.] Our hearts' desire and prayer to our heavenly Father every day should be, that he would <hi type="italic">forgive us our debts;</hi> that the obligation to punishment may be cancelled and vacated, that we may <hi type="italic">not come into condemnation;</hi> that we may be discharged, and have the comfort of it. In suing out the pardon of our sins, the great plea we have to rely upon is the satisfaction that was made to the justice of God for the sin of man, by the dying of the Lord Jesus our Surety, or rather Bail to the action, that undertook our discharge. <div eID="gen21614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21615" type="x-p"/> (2.) An argument to enforce this petition; <hi type="italic">as we forgive our debtors.</hi> This is not a plea of merit, but a plea of grace. Note, Those that come to God for the forgiveness of their sins against him, must make conscience of forgiving those who have offended them, else they curse themselves when they say the Lord's prayer. Our duty is to <hi type="italic">forgive our debtors;</hi> as to debts of money, we must not be rigorous and severe in exacting them from those that cannot pay them without ruining themselves and their families; but this means debt of injury; our debtors are those that <hi type="italic">trespass against us,</hi> that <hi type="italic">smite us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.39-Matt.5.40">ch. v. 39, 40</reference>), and in strictness of law, might be prosecuted for it; we must forbear, and forgive, and forget the affronts put upon us, and the wrongs done us; and this is a moral qualification for pardon and peace; it encourages to hope, that God will <hi type="italic">forgive us;</hi> for if there be in us this gracious disposition, it is wrought of God, and therefore is a perfection eminently and transcendently in himself; it will be an evidence to us that he has forgiven us, having wrought in us the condition of forgiveness. <div eID="gen21615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21616" type="x-p"/> 6. <hi type="italic">And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.</hi> This petition is expressed, <div eID="gen21616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21617" type="x-p"/> (1.) Negatively: <hi type="italic">Lead us not into temptation.</hi> Having prayed that the guilt of sin may be removed, we pray, as it is fit, that we may never return again to folly, that we may not be tempted to it. It is not as if God tempted any to sin; but, "Lord, do not let Satan loose upon us; chain up that <hi type="italic">roaring lion,</hi> for he is subtle and spiteful; Lord, do not leave us to ourselves (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.13">Ps. xix. 13</reference>), for we are very weak; Lord, do not <hi type="italic">lay stumbling-blocks</hi> and snares before us, nor put us into circumstances that may be <hi type="italic">an occasion of falling.</hi>" Temptations are to be prayed against, both because of the discomfort and trouble of them, and because of the danger we are in of being overcome by them, and the guilt and grief that then follow. <div eID="gen21617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21618" type="x-p"/> (2.) Positively: <hi type="italic">But deliver us from evil;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">apo tou ponerou</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">from the evil one,</hi> the devil, the tempter; "keep us, that either we may not be assaulted by him, or we may not be overcome by those assaults:" Or <hi type="italic">from the evil thing,</hi> sin, the worst of evils; an evil, an only evil; that evil thing which God hates, and which Satan tempts men to and destroys them by. "Lord, deliver us from the evil of the world, the corruption that is in the world through lust; from the evil of every condition in the world; from the evil of death; from the <hi type="italic">sting of death, which is sin:</hi> deliver us from ourselves, from our own evil hearts: deliver us from evil men, that they may not be a snare to us, nor we a prey to them." <div eID="gen21618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21619" type="x-p"/> III. The conclusion: <hi type="italic">For thine is the kingdom, and the power and the glory, for ever. Amen.</hi> Some refer this to David's doxology, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.11">1 Chron. xxix. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thine, O Lord, is the greatness.</hi> It is, <div eID="gen21619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21620" type="x-p"/> 1. A form of plea to enforce the foregoing petitions. It is our duty to plead with God in prayer, to fill our mouth with arguments (<reference osisRef="Job.23.4">Job xxiii. 4</reference>) not to move God, but to affect ourselves; to encourage the faith, to excite our fervency, and to evidence both. Now the best pleas in prayer are those that are taken from God himself, and from that which he has made known of himself. We must wrestle with God in his own strength, both as to the nature of our pleas and the urging of them. The plea here has special reference to the first three petitions; "<hi type="italic">Father in heaven, thy kingdom come, for thine is the kingdom; thy will be done, for thine is the power; hallowed be thy name, for thine is the glory.</hi>" And as to our own particular errands, these are encouraging: "<hi type="italic">Thine is the kingdom;</hi> thou hast the government of the world, and the protection of the saints, thy willing subjects in it;" God gives and saves like a king. "<hi type="italic">Thine is the power,</hi> to maintain and support that kingdom, and to make good all thine engagements to thy people." <hi type="italic">Thine is the glory,</hi> as the end of all that which is given to, and done for, the saints, in answer to their prayers; for their <hi type="italic">praise waiteth</hi> for him. This is matter of comfort and holy confidence in prayer. <div eID="gen21620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21621" type="x-p"/> 2. It is a form of praise and thanksgiving. The best pleading with God is praising of him; it is the way to obtain further mercy, as it qualifies us to receive it. In all our addresses to God, it is fit that praise should have a considerable share, for <hi type="italic">praise becometh the saints;</hi> they are to be our God <hi type="italic">for a name and for a praise.</hi> It is just and equal; we praise God, and give him glory, not because he needs it—he is praised by a world of angels, but because he deserves it; and it is our duty to give him glory, in compliance with his design in revealing himself to us. Praise is the work and happiness of heaven; and all that would go to heaven hereafter, must begin their heaven now. Observe, how full this doxology is, <hi type="italic">The kingdom, and the power, and the glory,</hi> it is all thine. Note, It becomes us to be copious in praising God. A true saint never thinks he can speak honourably enough of God: here there should be a gracious fluency, and this <hi type="italic">for ever.</hi> Ascribing glory to God <hi type="italic">for ever,</hi> intimates an acknowledgement, that it is eternally due, and an earnest desire to be eternally doing it, with angels and saints above, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.14">Ps. lxxi. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen21621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21622" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> To all this we are taught to affix our <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> so be it. God's <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> is a grant; his <hi type="italic">fiat</hi> is, it shall be so; our <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> is only a summary desire; our <hi type="italic">fiat</hi> is, let it be so: it is in the token of our desire and assurance to be heard, that we say <hi type="italic">Amen.</hi> <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> refers to every petition going before, and thus, in compassion to our infirmities, we are taught to knit up the whole in one word, and so to gather up, in the general, what we have lost and let slip in the particulars. It is good to conclude religious duties with some warmth and vigour, that we may go from them with a sweet savour upon our spirits. It was of old the practice of good people to say, <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> audibly at the end of every prayer, and it is a commendable practice, provided it be done with understanding, as the apostle directs (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.16">1 Cor. xiv. 16</reference>), and uprightly, with life and liveliness, and inward expressions, answerable to that outward expression of desire and confidence. <div eID="gen21622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21623" type="x-p"/> Most of the petitions in the Lord's prayer had been commonly used by the Jews in their devotions, or words to the same effect: but that clause in the fifth petition, <hi type="italic">As we forgive our debtors,</hi> was perfectly new, and therefore our Saviour here shows for what reason he added it, not with any personal reflection upon the peevishness, litigiousness, and ill nature of the men of that generation, though there was cause enough for it, but only from the necessity and importance of the thing itself. God, in forgiving us, has a peculiar respect to our forgiving those that have injured us; and therefore, when we pray for pardon, we must mention our making conscience of that duty, not only to remind ourselves of it, but to bind ourselves to it. See that parable, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.23-Matt.18.25">ch. xviii. 23-35</reference>. Selfish nature is loth to comply with this, and therefore it is here inculcated, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.14-Matt.6.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. <div eID="gen21623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21624" type="x-p"/> 1. In a promise. <hi type="italic">If ye forgive, your heavenly Father will also forgive.</hi> Not as if this were the only condition required; there must be repentance and faith, and new obedience; but as where other graces are in truth, there will be this, so this will be a good evidence of the sincerity of our other graces. He that relents toward his brother, thereby shows that he repents toward his God. Those which in the prayer are called <hi type="italic">debts,</hi> are here called <hi type="italic">trespasses, debts</hi> of injury, wrongs done to us in our bodies, goods, or reputation: <hi type="italic">trespasses</hi> is an extenuating term for offences, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">paraptomata</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">stumbles, slips, falls.</hi> Note, It is a good evidence, and a good help of our forgiving others, to call the injuries done us by a mollifying, excusing name. Call them not <hi type="italic">treasons,</hi> but <hi type="italic">trespasses;</hi> not wilful injuries, but casual inadvertencies; <hi type="italic">peradventure it was an oversight</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.43.12">Gen. xliii. 12</reference>), therefore make the best of it. We must forgive, as we hope to be forgiven; and therefore must not only bear no malice, nor mediate revenge, but must not upbraid our brother with the injuries he has done us, nor rejoice in any hurt that befals him, but must be ready to help him and do him good, and if he repent and desire to be friends again, we must be free and familiar with him, as before. <div eID="gen21624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21625" type="x-p"/> 2. In a threatening. "<hi type="italic">But if you forgive not</hi> those that have injured you, that is a bad sign you have not the other requisite conditions, but are altogether unqualified for pardon: and therefore <hi type="italic">your Father,</hi> whom you call Father, and who, as a father, offers you his grace upon reasonable terms, will nevertheless <hi type="italic">not forgive you.</hi> And if other grace be sincere, and yet you be defective greatly in forgiving, you cannot expect the comfort of your pardon, but to have your spirit brought down by some affliction or other to comply with this duty." Note, Those who would have found mercy with God must show mercy to their brethren; no can we expect that he should stretch out the hands of his favour to us, unless we lift up to him <hi type="italic">pure hands, without wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.8">1 Tim. ii. 8</reference>. If we pray in anger, we have reason to fear God will answer in anger. It has been said, Prayers made in wrath are written in gall. What reason is it that God should forgive us the talents we are indebted to him, if we forgive not our brethren the pence they are indebted to us? Christ <hi type="italic">came into the world</hi> as the great Peace-Maker, and not only <hi type="italic">to reconcile us to God,</hi> but one to another, and in this we must comply with him. It is great presumption and of dangerous consequence, for any to make a light matter of that which Christ here lays such a stress upon. Men's passions shall not frustrate God's word.
entries.6cef4513f77a8669a0513531a1ca4f1186453498: <div eID="gen21625" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21626" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward. <hi type="super">17</hi> But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; <hi type="super">18</hi> That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly. <div eID="gen21626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21627" type="x-p"/> We are here cautioned against hypocrisy in fasting, as before in almsgiving, and in prayer. <div eID="gen21627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21628" type="x-p"/> I. It is here supposed that religious fasting is a duty required of the disciples of Christ, when God, in his providence, calls to it, and when the case of their own souls upon any account requires it; <hi type="italic">when the bridegroom is taken away, then shall they fast,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.9.15">ch. ix. 15</reference>. Fasting is here put last, because it is not so much a duty for its own sake, as a means to dispose us for other duties. Prayer comes in between almsgiving and fasting, as being the life and soul of both. Christ here speaks especially of private fasts, such as particular persons prescribe to themselves, as free-will offerings, commonly used among the pious Jews; some fasted one day, some two, every week; others seldomer, as they saw cause. On those days they did not eat till sun-set, and then very sparingly. It was not the Pharisee's fasting <hi type="italic">twice in the week,</hi> but his boasting of it, that Christ condemned, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.12">Luke xviii. 12</reference>. It is a laudable practice, and we have reason to lament it, that is so generally neglected among Christians. Anna was much in fasting, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.37">Luke ii. 37</reference>. Cornelius fasted and prayed, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.30">Acts x. 30</reference>. The primitive Christians were much in it, see <reference osisRef="Acts.13.3">Acts xiii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.23">xiv. 23</reference>. Private fasting is supposed, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.5">1 Cor. vii. 5</reference>. It is an act of self-denial, and mortification of the flesh, a holy revenge upon ourselves, and humiliation under the hand of God. The most grown Christians must hereby own, they are so far from having any thing to be proud of, that they are unworthy of their daily bread. It is a means to curb the flesh and the desires of it, and to make us more lively in religious exercises, as fulness of bread is apt to make us drowsy. Paul was <hi type="italic">in fastings often,</hi> and so he <hi type="italic">kept under this body, and brought it into subjection.</hi> <div eID="gen21628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21629" type="x-p"/> II. We are cautioned not to do this <hi type="italic">as the hypocrites</hi> did it, lest we lose the reward of it; and the more difficulty attends the duty, the greater loss it is to lose the reward of it. <div eID="gen21629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21630" type="x-p"/> Now, 1. The <hi type="italic">hypocrites</hi> pretended fasting, when there was nothing of that contrition or humiliation of soul in them, which is the life and soul of the duty. Theirs were mock-fasts, the show and shadow without the substance; they took on them to be more humbled than really they were, and so endeavored to put a cheat upon God, than which they could not put a greater affront upon him. The fast that God has chosen, is <hi type="italic">a day to afflict the soul, not to hang down the head like a bulrush,</hi> nor for a man <hi type="italic">to spread sackcloth and ashes under him;</hi> we are quite mistaken if we call this a fast, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.5">Isa. lviii. 5</reference>. Bodily exercise, if that be all, profits little, since that is not fasting to God, even to him. <div eID="gen21630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21631" type="x-p"/> 2. They proclaimed their fasting, and managed it so that all who saw them might take notice that it was a fasting-day with them. Even on these days they appeared in the streets, whereas they should have been in their closets; and the affected a downcast look, a melancholy countenance, a slow and solemn pace; and perfectly disfigured themselves, that men might see how often they fasted, and might extol them as devout, mortified men. Note, It is sad that men, who have, in some measure, mastered their pleasure, which is sensual wickedness, should be ruined by their pride, which is spiritual wickedness, and no less dangerous. Here also <hi type="italic">they have their reward,</hi> that praise and applause of men which they court and covet so much; <hi type="italic">they have</hi> it, and it is their all. <div eID="gen21631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21632" type="x-p"/> III. We are directed how to manage a private fast; we must keep it in private, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.17-Matt.6.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. He does not tell us how often we must fast; circumstances vary, and wisdom is profitable therein to direct; the Spirit in the word has left that to the Spirit in the heart; but take this for a rule, whenever you undertake this duty, study therein to approve yourselves to God, and not to recommend yourselves to the good opinion of men; humility must evermore attend upon our humiliation. Christ does not direct to abate any thing of the reality of the fast; he does not say,"take a little meat, or a little drink, or a little cordial;" no, "let the body suffer, but lay aside the show and appearance of it; appear with thy ordinary countenance, guise, and dress; and while thou deniest thyself thy bodily refreshments, do it so as that it may not be taken notice of, no, not by those that are nearest to thee; look pleasant, <hi type="italic">anoint thine head and wash thy face,</hi> as thou dost on ordinary days, on purpose to conceal thy devotion; and thou shalt be no loser in the praise of it at last; for though it be not of men, it shall be of God." Fasting is the humbling of the soul (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.13">Ps. xxxv. 13</reference>), that is the inside of the duty; let that therefore be thy principal care, and as to the outside of it, covet not to let it be seen. If we be sincere in our solemn fasts, and humble, and trust God's omniscience for our witness, and his goodness for our reward, we shall find, both that he did <hi type="italic">see in secret,</hi> and will <hi type="italic">reward openly.</hi> Religious fasts, if rightly kept, will shortly be recompensed with an everlasting feast. Our acceptance with God in our private fasts should make us dead, both to the applause of men (we must not do the duty in hopes of this), and to the censures of men too (we must not decline the duty for fear of them). David's fasting was turned to his reproach, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.10">Ps. lxix. 10</reference>; and yet, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.13">v. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">As for me,</hi> let them say what they will of me, <hi type="italic">my prayer is unto thee in an acceptable time.</hi>
entries.68f847dc4db0f60be7813f3d6cdd324411af9998: <div eID="gen21632" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21633" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: <hi type="super">20</hi> But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: <hi type="super">21</hi> For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. <hi type="super">22</hi> The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light. <hi type="super">23</hi> But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great <hi type="italic">is</hi> that darkness! <hi type="super">24</hi> No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon. <div eID="gen21633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21634" type="x-p"/> Worldly-mindedness is as common and as fatal a symptom of hypocrisy as any other, for by no sin can Satan have a surer and faster hold of the soul, under the cloak of a visible and passable profession of religion, than by this; and therefore Christ, having warned us against coveting <hi type="italic">the praise of men,</hi> proceeds next to warn us against coveting the wealth of the world; in this also we must take heed, lest we be as the hypocrites are, and do as they do: the fundamental error that they are guilty of is, that they choose the world for <hi type="italic">their reward;</hi> we must therefore take heed of hypocrisy and worldly-mindedness, in the choice we make of our treasure, our end, and our masters. <div eID="gen21634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21635" type="x-p"/> I. In choosing the <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> we <hi type="italic">lay up.</hi> Something or other every man has which he makes his <hi type="italic">treasure,</hi> his portion, which his heart is upon, to which he carries all he can get, and which he depends upon for futurity. It is <hi type="italic">that good,</hi> that chief good, which Solomon speaks of with such an emphasis, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.3">Eccl. ii. 3</reference>. Something the soul will have, which it looks upon as the best thing, which it has a complacency and confidence in above other things. Now Christ designs not to deprive us of our treasure, but to direct us in the choice of it; and here we have, <div eID="gen21635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21636" type="x-p"/> 1. A <hi type="italic">good caution</hi> against making <hi type="italic">the things that are seen,</hi> that <hi type="italic">are temporal,</hi> our best things, and placing our happiness in them. <hi type="italic">Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth.</hi> Christ's disciples had left all to follow him, let them still keep in the same good mind. A <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> is an abundance of something that is in itself, at least in our opinion, precious and valuable, and likely to stand us in stead hereafter. Now we must <hi type="italic">not lay up our treasures on earth,</hi> that is, (1.) We must not count these things the best things, nor the most valuable in themselves, nor the most serviceable to us: we must not call them glory, as Laban's sons did, but see and own that they have no glory in comparison with <hi type="italic">the glory that excelleth.</hi> (2.) We must not covet an abundance of these things, nor be still grasping at more and more of them, and adding to them, as men do to that which is their treasure, as never knowing when we have enough.
