(3.) We must not confide in them for futurity, to be our security and supply in time to come; we must not say to the gold, <hi type="italic">Thou art my hope.</hi> (4.) We must not content ourselves with them, as all we need or desire: we must be content with a little for our passage, but not with all for our portion. These things must not be made <hi type="italic">our consolation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.24">Luke vi. 24</reference>), our <hi type="italic">good things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Luke xvi. 25</reference>. Let us consider we are laying up, not for our <hi type="italic">posterity</hi> in this world, but for <hi type="italic">ourselves</hi> in the other world. We are put to our choice, and made in a manner our own carvers; that is ours which <hi type="italic">we lay up for ourselves.</hi> It concerns thee to choose wisely, for thou art choosing for thyself, and shalt have as thou choosest. If we know and consider ourselves what we are, what we are made for, how large our capacities are, and how long our continuance, and that our souls are ourselves, we shall see it is foolish thing to <hi type="italic">lay up</hi> our <hi type="italic">treasures on earth.</hi> <div eID="gen21636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21637" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is a <hi type="italic">good reason</hi> given why we should not look upon any thing <hi type="italic">on earth</hi> as our <hi type="italic">treasure,</hi> because it is liable to loss and decay: (1.) From corruption within. That which is treasure <hi type="italic">upon earth moth and rust do corrupt.</hi> If the <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> be laid up in fine clothes, the <hi type="italic">moth</hi> frets them, and they are gone and spoiled insensibly, when we thought them most securely laid up. If it be in corn or other eatables, as his was who had his barns full (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.16-Luke.12.17">Luke xii. 16, 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">rust</hi> (so we read it) <hi type="italic">corrupts</hi> that: <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Brosis</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">eating,</hi> eating by men, for <hi type="italic">as goods are increased they are increased that eat them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11">Eccl. v. 11</reference>); eating by mice or other vermin; manna itself bred worms; or it grows mouldy and musty, is struck, or smutted, or blasted; fruits soon rot. Or, if we understand it of silver and gold, they tarnish and canker; they grow less with using, and grow worse with keeping (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.2-Jas.5.3">Jam. v. 2, 3</reference>); the <hi type="italic">rust and</hi> the <hi type="italic">moth</hi> breed in the metal itself and in the garment itself. Note, Worldly riches have in themselves a principal of corruption and decay; they wither of themselves, and <hi type="italic">make themselves wings.</hi> (2.) From violence without. <hi type="italic">Thieves break through and steal.</hi> Every hand of violence will be aiming at the house where <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> is laid up; nor can any thing be laid up so safe, but we may be spoiled of it. <hi type="italic">Numquam ego fortunæ credidi, etiam si videretur pacem agere; omnia illa quæ in me indulgentissime conferebat, pecuniam, honores, gloriam, eo loco posui, unde posset ea, since metu meo, repetere—I never reposed confidence in fortune, even if she seemed propitious: whatever were the favours which her bounty bestowed, whether wealth, honours, or glory, I so disposed of them, that it was in her power to recall them without occasioning me any alarm.</hi> Seneca. <hi type="italic">Consol. ad Helv.</hi> It is folly to make that our <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> which we may so easily be robbed of. <div eID="gen21637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21638" type="x-p"/> 3. <hi type="italic">Good counsel,</hi> to make the joys and glories of the other world, those <hi type="italic">things not seen</hi> that are <hi type="italic">eternal,</hi> our best things, and to place our happiness in them. <hi type="italic">Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven.</hi> Note, (1.) There are <hi type="italic">treasures in heaven,</hi> as sure as there are on this earth; and those in heaven are the only true <hi type="italic">treasures,</hi> the riches and glories and pleasures that are at God's right hand, which those that are sanctified truly arrive at, when they come to be sanctified perfectly. (2.) It is our wisdom to <hi type="italic">lay up</hi> our <hi type="italic">treasure in</hi> those <hi type="italic">treasures;</hi> to give all diligence to make sure our title to eternal life through Jesus Christ, and to depend upon that as our happiness, and look upon all things here below with a holy contempt, as not worthy to be compared with it. We must firmly believe there is such a happiness, and resolve to be content with that, and to be content with nothing short of it. If we thus make those <hi type="italic">treasures</hi> ours, they are laid up, and we may trust God to keep them safe for us; thither let us then refer all our designs, and extend all our desires; thither let us send before our best efforts and best affections. Let us not burthen ourselves with the cash of this world, which will but load and defile us, and be liable to sink us, but lay up in store good securities. The promises are bills of exchange, by which all true believers return their <hi type="italic">treasure to heaven,</hi> payable in the future state: and thus we make that sure that will be made sure. (3.) It is a great encouragement to us to <hi type="italic">lay up</hi> our <hi type="italic">treasure in heaven,</hi> that there it is safe; it will not decay of itself, no <hi type="italic">moth</hi> nor <hi type="italic">rust</hi> will <hi type="italic">corrupt</hi> it; nor can we be by force or fraud deprived of it; <hi type="italic">thieves do not break through and steal.</hi> It is a happiness above and beyond the changes and chances of time, <hi type="italic">an inheritance incorruptible.</hi> <div eID="gen21638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21639" type="x-p"/> 4. A <hi type="italic">good reason</hi> why we should thus choose, and an evidence that we have done so (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.21">v. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">Where your treasure is,</hi> on earth or in heaven, <hi type="italic">there will you heart be.</hi> We are therefore concerned to be right and wise in the choice of our <hi type="italic">treasure,</hi> because the temper of our minds, and consequently the tenor of our lives, will be accordingly either carnal or spiritual, earthly or heavenly. The <hi type="italic">heart</hi> follows the <hi type="italic">treasure,</hi> as the needle follows the loadstone, or the sunflower the sun. <hi type="italic">Where the treasure is there</hi> the value and esteem are, <hi type="italic">there</hi> the love and affection are (<reference osisRef="Col.3.2">Col. iii. 2</reference>), that way the desires and pursuits go, thitherward the aims and intents are levelled, and all is done with that in view. <hi type="italic">Where the treasure is, there</hi> our cares and fears are, lest we come short of it; about that we are most solicitous; <hi type="italic">there</hi> our hope and trust are (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.10-Prov.18.11">Prov. xviii. 10, 11</reference>); <hi type="italic">there</hi> our joys and delights will be (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.111">Ps. cxix. 111</reference>); and <hi type="italic">there</hi> our thoughts will be, there the <hi type="italic">inward</hi> thought will be, the <hi type="italic">first</hi> thought, the <hi type="italic">free</hi> thought, the <hi type="italic">fixed</hi> thought, the <hi type="italic">frequent,</hi> the <hi type="italic">familiar</hi> thought. The <hi type="italic">heart</hi> is God's due (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.26">Prov. xxiii. 26</reference>), and that he may have it, our <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> must be laid up with him, and then our souls will be lifted up to him. <div eID="gen21639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21640" type="x-p"/> This direction about laying up our <hi type="italic">treasure,</hi> may very fitly be applied to the foregoing caution, of not doing what we do in religion <hi type="italic">to be seen of men.</hi> Our <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> is our alms, prayers, and fastings, and the reward of them; if we have done these only to gain the applause of men, we have <hi type="italic">laid up this treasure on earth,</hi> have lodged it in the hands of men, and must never expect to hear any further of it. Now it is folly to do this, for <hi type="italic">the praise of men</hi> we covet so much is liable to corruption: it will soon be rusted, and moth-eaten, and tarnished; a little folly, like a dead fly, will spoil it all, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.1">Eccl. x. 1</reference>. Slander and calumny are <hi type="italic">thieves that break through and steal</hi> it away, and so we lose all the <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> of our performances; we have run in vain, and laboured in vain, because we misplaced our intentions in doing of them. Hypocritical services lay up nothing in heaven (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.3">Isa. lviii. 3</reference>); the gain of them is gone, when the soul is called for, <reference osisRef="Job.27.8">Job xxvii. 8</reference>. But if we have prayed and fasted and given alms in truth and uprightness, with an eye to God and to his acceptance, and have approved ourselves to him therein, we have laid up that treasure <hi type="italic">in heaven; a book of remembrance is written there</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.16">Mal. iii. 16</reference>), and being there recorded, they shall be there rewarded, and we shall meet them again with comfort on the other side death and the grave. Hypocrites are <hi type="italic">written in the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.13">Jer. xvii. 13</reference>), but God's faithful ones have their names <hi type="italic">written in heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.10.20">Luke x. 20</reference>. Acceptance with God is <hi type="italic">treasure in heaven,</hi> which can neither be corrupted nor stolen. His <hi type="italic">well done</hi> shall stand for ever; and if we have thus laid up our <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> with him, with him our <hi type="italic">hearts</hi> will be; and where can they be better? <div eID="gen21640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21641" type="x-p"/> II. We must take heed of hypocrisy and worldly-mindedness in choosing the <hi type="italic">end we look at.</hi> Our concern as to this is represented by two sorts of eyes which men have, a <hi type="italic">single eye</hi> and an <hi type="italic">evil eye,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.22-Matt.6.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. The expressions here are somewhat dark because concise; we shall therefore take them in some variety of interpretation. <hi type="italic">The light of the body is the eye,</hi> that is plain; <hi type="italic">the eye</hi> is discovering and directing; the <hi type="italic">light of the world</hi> would avail us little without this <hi type="italic">light of the body;</hi> it is <hi type="italic">the light of the eye</hi> that <hi type="italic">rejoiceth the heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.15.30">Prov. xv. 30</reference>), but what is that which is here compared to <hi type="italic">the eye</hi> in the <hi type="italic">body.</hi> <div eID="gen21641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21642" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">The eye,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">the heart</hi> (so some) if that <hi type="italic">be single</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">haplous</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">free and bountiful</hi> (so the word is frequently rendered, as <reference osisRef="Rom.12.8 2Cor.8.2 2Cor.9.11 2Cor.9.13">Rom. xii. 8; 2 Cor. viii. 2, ix. 11, 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.5">Jam. i. 5</reference>, and we read of a <hi type="italic">bountiful eye,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.22.9">Prov. xxii. 9</reference>). If the heart be liberally affected and stand inclined to goodness and charity, it will direct the man to Christian actions, the whole conversation <hi type="italic">will be full of light,</hi> full of evidences and instances of true Christianity, that <hi type="italic">pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.27">Jam. i. 27</reference>), <hi type="italic">full of light,</hi> of good works, which are our <hi type="italic">light shining before men;</hi> but <hi type="italic">if the heart be evil,</hi> covetous, and hard, and envious, griping and grudging (such a temper of mind is often expressed by an <hi type="italic">evil eye,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.20.15">ch. xx. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.7.22">Mark vii. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.7.22">Prov. xxiii. 6, 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">the body will be full of darkness,</hi> the whole conversation will be heathenish and unchristian. <hi type="italic">The instruments of the churl are</hi> and always will be <hi type="italic">evil,</hi> but <hi type="italic">the liberal deviseth liberal things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.5-Isa.32.8">Isa. xxxii. 5-8</reference>. <hi type="italic">If the light that is in us,</hi> those affections which should guide us to that which is good, <hi type="italic">be darkness,</hi> if these be corrupt and worldly, if there be not so much as good nature in a man, not so much as a kind disposition, <hi type="italic">how great is</hi> the corruption of a man, and the <hi type="italic">darkness</hi> in which he sits! This sense seems to agree with the context; we must <hi type="italic">lay up treasure in heaven</hi> by liberality in giving alms, and that not grudgingly but with cheerfulness, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.33">Luke xii. 33</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.7">2 Cor. ix. 7</reference>. But these words in the parallel place do not come in upon any such occasion, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.34">Luke xi. 34</reference>, and therefore the coherence here does not determine that to be the sense of them. <div eID="gen21642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21643" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">The eye,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">the understanding</hi> (so some); the practical judgment, the conscience, which is to the other faculties of the soul, as <hi type="italic">the eye</hi> is to the <hi type="italic">body,</hi> to guide and direct their motions; now <hi type="italic">if this eye be single,</hi> if it make a true and right judgment, and discern things that differ, especially in the great concern of <hi type="italic">laying up the treasure</hi> so as to choose aright in that, it will rightly guide the affections and actions, which will all be <hi type="italic">full of the light</hi> of grace and comfort; <hi type="italic">but if this be evil</hi> and corrupt, and instead of leading the inferior powers, is led, and bribed, and biassed by them, if this be erroneous and misinformed, the heart and life must needs be <hi type="italic">full of darkness,</hi> and the whole conversation corrupt. They that <hi type="italic">will not understand,</hi> are said to <hi type="italic">walk on in darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Ps. lxxxii. 5</reference>. It is sad when the spirit of a man, that should be <hi type="italic">the candle of the Lord,</hi> is an <hi type="italic">ignis fatuus:</hi> when the <hi type="italic">leaders of the people,</hi> the leaders of the faculties, <hi type="italic">cause them to err,</hi> for then <hi type="italic">they that are led of them are destroyed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.9.16">Isa. ix. 16</reference>. An error in the practical judgment is fatal, it is that which calls <hi type="italic">evil good and good evil</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.20">Isa. v. 20</reference>); therefore it concerns us to understand things aright, to get our eyes anointed with eye-salve. <div eID="gen21643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21644" type="x-p"/> 3. <hi type="italic">The eye,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">the aims</hi> and <hi type="italic">intentions;</hi> by <hi type="italic">the eye</hi> we set our end before us, the mark we shoot at, the place we go to, we keep that in view, and direct our motion accordingly; in every thing we do in religion; there is something or other that we have in our <hi type="italic">eye;</hi> now <hi type="italic">if our eye be single,</hi> if we aim honestly, fix right ends, and move rightly towards them, if we aim purely and only at the glory of God, seek his honor and favour, and direct all entirely to him, then <hi type="italic">the eye is single;</hi> Paul's was so when he said, <hi type="italic">To me to live is Christ;</hi> and if we be right here, <hi type="italic">the whole body will be full of light,</hi> all the actions will be regular and gracious, pleasing to God and comfortable to ourselves; <hi type="italic">but if this eye be evil,</hi> if, instead of aiming only at the glory of God, and our acceptance with him, we look aside at the applause of men, and while we profess to honour God, contrive to honour ourselves, and seek our own things under colour of <hi type="italic">seeking the things of Christ,</hi> this spoils all, the whole conversation will be perverse and unsteady, and the foundations being thus out of course, there can be nothing but <hi type="italic">confusion and every evil work</hi> in the superstructure. Draw the lines from the circumference to any other point but the centre, and they will cross. <hi type="italic">If the light that is in thee be</hi> not only dim, but <hi type="italic">darkness</hi> itself, it is a fundamental error, and destructive to all that follows. The end specifies the action. It is of the last importance in religion, that we be right in our aims, and make <hi type="italic">eternal things,</hi> not <hi type="italic">temporal,</hi> our scope, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.18">2 Cor. iv. 18</reference>. The hypocrite is like the waterman, that looks one way and rows another; the true Christian like the traveller, that has his journey's end in his eye. The hypocrite soars like the kite, with his eye upon the prey below, which he is ready to come down to when he has a fair opportunity; the true Christian soars like the lark, higher and higher, forgetting the things that are beneath. <div eID="gen21644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21645" type="x-p"/> III. We must take heed of hypocrisy and worldly-mindedness in choosing the master we serve, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.24">v. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">No man can serve two masters.</hi> Serving <hi type="italic">two masters</hi> is contrary to <hi type="italic">the single eye;</hi> for <hi type="italic">the eye</hi> will be to the master's hand, <reference osisRef="Ps.123.1-Ps.123.2">Ps. cxxiii. 1, 2</reference>. Our Lord Jesus here exposes the cheat which those put upon their own souls, who think to divide between God and the world, to have a <hi type="italic">treasure on earth,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">treasure in heaven</hi> too, to please God and please men too. Why not? says the hypocrite; it is good to have two strings to one's bow. They hope to make their religion serve their secular interest, and so turn to account both ways. The pretending mother was for dividing the child; the Samaritans will compound between God and idols. No, says Christ, this will not do; it is but a supposition that <hi type="italic">gain is godliness,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.5">1 Tim. vi. 5</reference>. Here is, <div eID="gen21645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21646" type="x-p"/> 1. A general maxim laid down; it is likely it was a proverb among the Jews, <hi type="italic">No man can serve two masters,</hi> much less two gods; for their commands will some time or other cross or contradict one another, and their occasions interfere. While <hi type="italic">two masters</hi> go together, a servant may follow them both; but when they part, you will see to which he belongs; he cannot love, and observe, and cleave to both as he should. If to the one, not to the other; either this or that must be comparatively hated and despised. This truth is plain enough in common cases. <div eID="gen21646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21647" type="x-p"/> 2. The application of it to the business in hand. <hi type="italic">Ye cannot serve God and Mammon.</hi> <hi type="italic">Mammon</hi> is a Syriac word, that signifies gain; so that whatever in this world is, or is accounted by us to be, <hi type="italic">gain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.7">Phil. iii. 7</reference>), is <hi type="italic">mammon. Whatever is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eye, and the pride of life,</hi> is <hi type="italic">mammon.</hi> To some their belly is their <hi type="italic">mammon,</hi> and they serve that (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Phil. iii. 19</reference>); to others their ease, their sleep, their sports and pastimes, are their <hi type="italic">mammon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.9">Prov. vi. 9</reference>); to others worldly riches (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.13">James iv. 13</reference>); to others honours and preferments; the praise and applause of men was the Pharisees' <hi type="italic">mammon;</hi> in a word, self, the unity in which the world's trinity centres, sensual, secular self, is the <hi type="italic">mammon</hi> which cannot be served in conjunction with <hi type="italic">God;</hi> for if it be served, it is in competition with him and in contradiction to him. He does not say, We <hi type="italic">must</hi> not or we <hi type="italic">should</hi> not, but we <hi type="italic">cannot serve God and Mammon;</hi> we <hi type="italic">cannot</hi> love both (<reference osisRef="1John.2.15">1 John ii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.4">Jam. iv. 4</reference>); or hold to both, or hold by both in observance, obedience, attendance, trust, and dependence, for they are contrary the one to the other. <hi type="italic">God</hi> says, "<hi type="italic">My son, give me thy heart.</hi>" <hi type="italic">Mammon</hi> says, "No, give it me." <hi type="italic">God</hi> says, "<hi type="italic">Be content with such things as ye have.</hi>" <hi type="italic">Mammon</hi> says, "Grasp at all that ever thou canst. <hi type="italic">Rem, rem, quocunque modo rem—Money, money; by fair means or by foul, money.</hi>" <hi type="italic">God</hi> says, "Defraud not, never lie, be honest and just in all thy dealings." <hi type="italic">Mammon</hi> says "Cheat thine own Father, if thou canst gain by it." <hi type="italic">God</hi> says, "Be charitable." <hi type="italic">Mammon</hi> says, "Hold thy own: this giving undoes us all." <hi type="italic">God</hi> says, "<hi type="italic">Be careful for nothing.</hi>" <hi type="italic">Mammon</hi> says, "Be careful for every thing." <hi type="italic">God</hi> says, "<hi type="italic">Keep holy thy sabbath-day.</hi>" <hi type="italic">Mammon</hi> says, "Make use of that day as well as any other for the world." Thus inconsistent are the commands of <hi type="italic">God and Mammon,</hi> so that we <hi type="italic">cannot serve</hi> both. Let us not then <hi type="italic">halt between God and Baal, but choose ye this day whom ye will serve,</hi> and abide by our choice.
entries.50a4ef825d5bd26a3571d83c10ce0eb3eb62c43a: <div eID="gen21647" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21648" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment? <hi type="super">26</hi> Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they? <hi type="super">27</hi> Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature? <hi type="super">28</hi> And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin: <hi type="super">29</hi> And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. <hi type="super">30</hi> Wherefore, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, <hi type="italic">shall he</hi> not much more <hi type="italic">clothe</hi> you, O ye of little faith? <hi type="super">31</hi> Therefore take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or, What shall we drink? or, Wherewithal shall we be clothed? <hi type="super">32</hi> (For after all these things do the Gentiles seek:) for your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things. <hi type="super">33</hi> But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you. <hi type="super">34</hi> Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day <hi type="italic">is</hi> the evil thereof. <div eID="gen21648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21649" type="x-p"/> There is scarcely any one sin against which our Lord Jesus more largely and earnestly warns his disciples, or against which he arms them with more variety of arguments, than the sin of disquieting, distracting, distrustful cares about the things of life, which are a bad sign that both the <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> and the heart are <hi type="italic">on the earth;</hi> and therefore he thus largely insists upon it. Here is, <div eID="gen21649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21650" type="x-p"/> I. The prohibition laid down. It is the counsel and command of the Lord Jesus, that we <hi type="italic">take no thought</hi> about the things of this world; <hi type="italic">I say unto you.</hi> He says it as our Lawgiver, and the Sovereign of our hearts; he says it as our Comforter, and the Helper of our joy. What is it that he says? It is this, and <hi type="italic">he that hath ears to hear, let him hear it. Take no thought for your life, nor yet for your body</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.25">v. 25</reference>). <hi type="italic">Take no thought, saying, What shall we eat?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.31">v. 31</reference>) and again (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.34">v. 34</reference>), <hi type="italic">Take no thought,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">me merimnate</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Be not in care.</hi> As against hypocrisy, so against worldly cares, the caution is thrice repeated, and yet no vain repetition: <hi type="italic">precept</hi> must be <hi type="italic">upon precept, and line upon line,</hi> to the same purport, and all little enough; it is a <hi type="italic">sin which doth so easily beset us.</hi> It intimates how pleasing it is to Christ, and of how much concern it is to ourselves, that we should live without carefulness. It is the repeated command of the Lord Jesus to his disciples, that they should not divide and pull in pieces their own minds with care about the world. There is a <hi type="italic">thought</hi> concerning the things of this life, which is not only lawful, but duty, such as is commended in the virtuous woman. See <reference osisRef="Prov.27.23">Prov. xxvii. 23</reference>. The word is used concerning Paul's care of the churches, and Timothy's care for the state of souls, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.28">2 Cor. xi. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.20">Phil. ii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen21650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21651" type="x-p"/> But the <hi type="italic">thought</hi> here forbidden is, 1. A disquieting, tormenting <hi type="italic">thought,</hi> which hurries the mind hither and thither, and hangs it in suspense; which disturbs our joy in God, and is a damp upon our hope in him; which breaks the sleep, and hinders our enjoyment of ourselves, of our friends, and of what God has given us. 2. A distrustful, unbelieving <hi type="italic">thought.</hi> God has promised to provide for those that are his all things needful for life as well as godliness, <hi type="italic">the life that now is,</hi> food and a covering: not dainties, but necessaries. He never said, "They shall be feasted," but, "<hi type="italic">Verily, they shall be fed.</hi>" Now an inordinate care for time to come, and fear of wanting those supplies, spring from a disbelief of these promises, and of the wisdom and goodness of Divine Providence; and that is the evil of it. As to present sustenance, we may and must use lawful means to get it, else we tempt God; we must be diligent in our callings, and prudent in proportioning our expenses to what we have, and we must pray for <hi type="italic">daily bread;</hi> and if all other means fail, we may and must ask relief of those that are able to give it. He was none of the best of men that said, <hi type="italic">To beg I am ashamed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.3">Luke xvi. 3</reference>); as he was, who (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.21">v. 21</reference>) <hi type="italic">desired to be fed with the crumbs;</hi> but for the future, we must <hi type="italic">cast our care upon God,</hi> and <hi type="italic">take no thought,</hi> because it looks like a jealousy of God, who knows how to give what we want when we know not now to get it. Let our souls dwell at ease in him! This gracious carelessness is the same with that sleep which God gives to his beloved, in opposition to the worldling's toil, <reference osisRef="Ps.127.2">Ps. cxxvii. 2</reference>. Observe the cautions here, <div eID="gen21651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21652" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">Take no thought for your life.</hi> Life is our greatest concern for this world; <hi type="italic">All that a man has will he give for his life;</hi> yet take no thought about it. [1.] Not about the <hi type="italic">continuance</hi> of it; refer it to God to <hi type="italic">lengthen</hi> or <hi type="italic">shorten</hi> it as he pleases; <hi type="italic">my times are in thy hand,</hi> and they are in a good hand. [2.] Not about the <hi type="italic">comforts</hi> of this life; refer it to God to embitter or sweeten it as he pleases. We must not be solicitous, no not about the necessary support of this life, <hi type="italic">food</hi> and <hi type="italic">raiment;</hi> these God has promised, and therefore we may more confidently expect; say not, <hi type="italic">What shall we eat?</hi> It is the language of one at a loss, and almost despairing; whereas, though many good people have the prospect of little, yet there are few but have present support. <div eID="gen21652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21653" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">Take no thought for the morrow,</hi> for the time to come. Be not solicitous for the future, how you shall live next year, or when you are old, or what you shall leave behind you. As we must not <hi type="italic">boast</hi> of to-morrow, so we must not <hi type="italic">care for</hi> to-morrow, or the events of it. <div eID="gen21653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21654" type="x-p"/> II. The reasons and arguments to enforce this prohibition. One would think the command of Christ was enough to restrain us from this foolish sin of disquieting, distrustful care, independently of the comfort of our own souls, which is so nearly concerned; but to show how much the heart of Christ is upon it, and what <hi type="italic">pleasures he takes</hi> in those that <hi type="italic">hope in his mercy,</hi> the command is backed with the most powerful arguments. If reason may but rule us, surely we shall ease ourselves of these thorns. To free us from anxious thoughts, and to expel them, Christ here suggests to us <hi type="italic">comforting</hi> thoughts, that we may be filled with them. It will be worth while to take pains with our own hearts, to argue them out of their disquieting cares, and to make ourselves ashamed of them. They may be weakened by right reason, but it is by an active faith only that they can be overcome. Consider then, <div eID="gen21654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21655" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.25">v. 25</reference>. Yes, no doubt it is; so he says who had reason to understand the true value of present things, for he made them, he supports them, and supports us by them; and the thing speaks for itself. Note, (1.) Our <hi type="italic">life</hi> is a greater blessing than our <hi type="italic">livelihood.</hi> It is true, life cannot subsist without a livelihood; but the meat and raiment which are here represented as inferior to the life and body are such as are for ornament and delight; for about such as are for ornament ad delight; for about such we are apt to be solicitous. Meat and raiment are in order to life, and the <hi type="italic">end</hi> is more noble and excellent than the <hi type="italic">means.</hi> The daintiest food and finest raiment are from the <hi type="italic">earth,</hi> but life from the <hi type="italic">breath of God.</hi> Life is the <hi type="italic">light of men;</hi> meat is but the <hi type="italic">oil</hi> that feeds that light: so that the difference between rich and poor is very inconsiderable, since, in the greatest things, they stand on the same level, and differ only in the less. (2.) This is an encouragement to us to trust God for <hi type="italic">food</hi> and <hi type="italic">raiment,</hi> and so to ease ourselves of all perplexing cares about them. God has given us life, and given us the body; it was an act of power, it was an act of favour, it was done without our care: what cannot he do for us, who did that?—what will he not? If we take care about our souls and eternity, which are more than the body, and its life, we may leave it to God to provide for us food and raiment, which are less. God has maintained our lives hitherto; if sometimes with pulse and water, that has answered the end; he has protected us and kept us alive. He that guards us against the evils we are exposed to, will supply us with the <hi type="italic">good things</hi> we are in need of. If he had been pleased to kill us, to starve us, he would not so often have <hi type="italic">given his angels a charge concerning us</hi> to keep us. <div eID="gen21655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21656" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">Behold the fowls of the air,</hi> and <hi type="italic">consider the lilies of the field.</hi> Here is an argument taken from God's common providence toward the inferior creatures, and their dependence, according to their capacities, upon that providence. A fine pass fallen man has come to, that he must be sent to school to the <hi type="italic">fowls of the air,</hi> and that they must <hi type="italic">teach him!</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.12.7-Job.12.8">Job xii. 7, 8</reference>. <div eID="gen21656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21657" type="x-p"/> (1.) Look upon the <hi type="italic">fowls,</hi> and learn to trust God <hi type="italic">for food</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.26">v. 26</reference>), and disquiet not yourselves with thoughts <hi type="italic">what you shall eat.</hi> <div eID="gen21657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21658" type="x-p"/> [1.] Observe the providence of God concerning them. Look upon them, and receive instruction. There are various sorts of fowls; they are numerous, some of them ravenous, but they are all fed, and fed with food convenient for them; it is rare that any of them perish for want of food, even in winter, and there goes no little to feed them all the year round. The fowls, as they are least serviceable to man, so they are least within his care; men often feed upon them, but seldom feed them; yet they are fed, we know not how, and some of them fed best in the hardest weather; and it is <hi type="italic">your heavenly Father that feeds them;</hi> he <hi type="italic">knows all the wild fowls of the mountains,</hi> better than you know the tame ones at your own barn-door, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.11">Ps. l. 11</reference>. Not a sparrow lights to the ground, to pick up a grain of corn, but by the providence of God, which extends itself to the meanest creatures. But that which is especially observed here is, that they are fed without any care or project of their own; <hi type="italic">they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns.</hi> The ant indeed does, and the bee, and they are set before us as examples of prudence and industry; but the fowls of the air do not; they make no provision for the future themselves, and yet every day, as duly as the day comes, provision is made for them, and their <hi type="italic">eyes wait on God,</hi> that great and good Housekeeper, who <hi type="italic">provides food for all flesh.</hi> <div eID="gen21658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21659" type="x-p"/> [2.] Improve this for your encouragement to trust in God. <hi type="italic">Are ye not much better than they?</hi> Yes, certainly you are. Note, The <hi type="italic">heirs</hi> of heaven are much better than the <hi type="italic">fowls</hi> of heaven; nobler and more excellent beings, and, by faith, they soar higher; they are of a better nature and nurture, <hi type="italic">wiser than the fowls of heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.35.11">Job xxxv. 11</reference>): though the children of this world, that <hi type="italic">know not the judgment of the Lord,</hi> are not so wise as <hi type="italic">the stork, and the crane, and the swallow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.7">Jer. viii. 7</reference>), you are dearer to God, and nearer, though they fly in the open firmament of heaven. He is their Master and Lord, their Owner and Master; but besides all this, he is your Father, and in his account <hi type="italic">ye are of more value than many sparrows;</hi> you are his children, his first-born; now he that feeds his birds surely will not starve his babes. They trust your Father's providence, and will not you trust it? In dependence upon that, they are careless for the morrow; and being so, they live the merriest lives of all creatures; they <hi type="italic">sing among the branches</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.12">Ps. civ. 12</reference>), and, to the best of their power, they praise their Creator. If we were, by faith, as unconcerned about the morrow as they are, we should sing as cheerfully as they do; for it is worldly care that mars our mirth and damps our joy, and silences our praise, as much as any thing. <div eID="gen21659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21660" type="x-p"/> (2.) Look upon the <hi type="italic">lilies,</hi> and learn to trust God for <hi type="italic">raiment.</hi> That is another part of our care, <hi type="italic">what we shall put on;</hi> for decency, to cover us; for defence, to keep us warm; yea, and, with many, for dignity and ornament, to make them look great and fine; and so much concerned are they for gaiety and variety in their clothing, that this care returns almost as often as that for their daily bread. Now to ease us of this care, let us <hi type="italic">consider the lilies of the field;</hi> not only <hi type="italic">look upon</hi> them (every eyes does that with pleasure), but <hi type="italic">consider</hi> them. Note, There is a great deal of good to be learned from what we see every day, if we would but consider it, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.6">Prov. vi. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.32">xxiv. 32</reference>. <div eID="gen21660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21661" type="x-p"/> [1.] Consider how <hi type="italic">frail</hi> the lilies are; they are the <hi type="italic">grass of the field.</hi> Lilies, though distinguished by their colours, are still but <hi type="italic">grass.</hi> Thus <hi type="italic">all flesh is grass:</hi> though some in the endowments of body and mind are as lilies, much admired, still they are grass; the grass of the field in nature and constitution; they stand upon the same level with others. Man's days, at best, are <hi type="italic">as grass,</hi> as the <hi type="italic">flower of the grass</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.24">1 Pet. i. 24</reference>. This grass <hi type="italic">to-day is,</hi> and <hi type="italic">to-morrow is cast into the oven;</hi> in a little while the place that <hi type="italic">knows us</hi> will <hi type="italic">know us no more.</hi> The grave is the oven into which we shall be cast, and in which we shall be consumed as grass in the fire, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Ps. xlix. 14</reference>. This intimates a reason why we should not take thought for the morrow, what we shall put on, because perhaps, by to-morrow, we may have occasion for our grave-clothes. <div eID="gen21661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21662" type="x-p"/> [2.] Consider how <hi type="italic">free from care</hi> the lilies are: they <hi type="italic">toil not</hi> as men do, to earn clothing; as servants, to earn their liveries; <hi type="italic">neither do they spin,</hi> as women do, to make clothing. It does not follow that we must therefore neglect, or do carelessly, the proper business of this life; it is the praise of the virtuous woman, that <hi type="italic">she lays her hand to the spindle, makes fine linen and sells it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.19">Prov. xxxi. 19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.24">24</reference>. Idleness <hi type="italic">tempts</hi> God, instead of <hi type="italic">trusting</hi> him; but he that provides for inferior creatures, without their labour, will much more provide for us, by blessing our labour, which he has made our duty. And if we should, through sickness, be unable to <hi type="italic">toil</hi> and <hi type="italic">spin,</hi> God can furnish us with what is necessary for us. <div eID="gen21662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21663" type="x-p"/> [3.] Consider how <hi type="italic">fair,</hi> how <hi type="italic">fine</hi> the lilies are; <hi type="italic">how they grow;</hi> what they <hi type="italic">grow from.</hi> The root of the lily or tulip, as other bulbous roots, is, in winter, lost and buried under ground, yet, when spring returns, it appears, and starts up in a little time; hence it is promised to God's Israel, that they should grow <hi type="italic">as the lily,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.14.5">Hos. xiv. 5</reference>. Consider what they <hi type="italic">grow to.</hi> Out of that obscurity in a few weeks they come to be so very gay, that even <hi type="italic">Solomon, in all his glory, was not arrayed like one of these.</hi> The array of Solomon was very splendid and magnificent: he that had the peculiar treasure of kings and provinces, and studiously affected pomp and gallantry, doubtless had the richest clothing, and the best made up, that could be got; especially when he appeared in his glory on high days. And yet, let him dress himself as fine as he could, he comes far short of the beauty of the lilies, and a bed of tulips outshines him. Let us, therefore, be ambitious of the <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> of Solomon, in which he was outdone by none (wisdom to do our duty in our places), rather than the <hi type="italic">glory</hi> of Solomon, in which he was outdone by the lilies. Knowledge and grace are the perfection of man, not beauty, much less fine clothes. Now God is here said thus to <hi type="italic">clothe the grass of the field.</hi> Note, All the excellences of the creature flow from God, the Fountain and spring of them. It was he that gave the horse his strength, and the lily its beauty; every creature is in itself, as well as to us, what he makes it to be. <div eID="gen21663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21664" type="x-p"/> [4.] Consider how instructive all this is to us, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.30">v. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen21664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21665" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As to <hi type="italic">fine</hi> clothing, this teaches us not to care for it at all, not to covet it, nor to be proud of it, not to make the <hi type="italic">putting on of apparel</hi> our <hi type="italic">adorning,</hi> for after all our care in this the lilies will far outdo us; we cannot dress so fine as they do, why then should we attempt to vie with them? Their adorning will soon perish, and so will ours; they fade—<hi type="italic">are to-day,</hi> and <hi type="italic">to-morrow are cast,</hi> as other rubbish, <hi type="italic">into the oven;</hi> and the clothes we are proud of are wearing out, the gloss is soon gone, the color fades, the shape goes out of fashion, or in awhile the garment itself is worn out; such is man in all his pomp (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.6-Isa.40.7">Isa. xl. 6, 7</reference>), especially rich men (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.10">Jam. i. 10</reference>); they <hi type="italic">fade away in their ways.</hi> <div eID="gen21665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21666" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> As to <hi type="italic">necessary</hi> clothing; this teaches us to cast the care of it upon God—Jehovah-jireh; trust him that clothes the lilies, to provide for you what you shall <hi type="italic">put on.</hi> If he give such fine clothes to the grass, much more will he give fitting clothes to his own children; clothes that shall be warm upon them, not only <hi type="italic">when he quieteth the earth with the south wind,</hi> but when he disquiets it with the <hi type="italic">north wind,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.37.17">Job xxxvii. 17</reference>. He shall much more clothe you: for you are nobler creatures, of a more excellent being; if so he clothe the short-lived grass, much more will he clothe you that are made for immortality. Even the children of Nineveh are preferred before the gourd (<reference osisRef="Jonah.4.10-Jonah.4.11">Jonah iv. 10, 11</reference>), much more the sons of Zion, that are in covenant with God. Observe the title he gives them (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.30">v. 30</reference>), <hi type="italic">O ye of little faith.</hi> This may be taken, 1. As an encouragement to truth faith, though it be but weak; it entitles us to the divine care, and a promise of suitable supply. Great faith shall be commended, and shall procure great things, but little faith shall not be rejected, even that shall procure food and raiment. <hi type="italic">Sound</hi> believers shall be provided for, though they be not <hi type="italic">strong</hi> believers. The babes in the family are fed and clothed, as well as those that are grown up, and with a special care and tenderness; say not, I am but a child, but a dry tree (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.3">Isa. lvi. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.5">5</reference>), for though <hi type="italic">poor and needy</hi> yet <hi type="italic">the Lord thinketh on thee.</hi> Or, 2. It is rather a rebuke to weak faith, though it be true, <reference osisRef="Matt.14.31">ch. xiv. 31</reference>. It intimates what is at the bottom of all our inordinate care and thoughtfulness; it is owing to the weakness of our faith, and the remains of unbelief in us. If we had but more faith, we should have less care. <div eID="gen21666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21667" type="x-p"/> 3. <hi type="italic">Which of you,</hi> the wisest, the strongest of you, <hi type="italic">by taking thought, can add one cubit to his stature?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.27">v. 27</reference>) to <hi type="italic">his age,</hi> so some; but the measure of a cubit denotes it to be meant of the stature, and the age at longest is but a span, <reference osisRef="Ps.39.5">Ps. xxxix. 5</reference>. Let us consider, (1.) We did not arrive at the stature we are of by our own care and thought, but by the providence of God. An infant of a span long has grown up to be a man of six feet, and how was one cubit after another added to his stature? not by his own forecast or contrivance; he grew he knew not how, by the power and goodness of God. Now he that made our bodies, and made them of such size, surely will take care to provide for them. Note, God is to be acknowledged in the increase of our bodily strength and stature, and to be trusted for all needful supplies, because he has made it to appear, that he is mindful for the body. The growing age is the thoughtless, careless age, yet we grow; and shall not he who reared us to this, provide for us now we are reared? (2.) We cannot alter the stature we are of, if we would: what a foolish and ridiculous thing would it be for a man of low stature to perplex himself, to break his sleep, and beat his brains, about it, and to be continually taking thought how he might be a cubit higher; when, after all, he knows he cannot effect it, and therefore he had better be content and take it as it is! We are not all of a size, yet the difference in stature between one and another is not material, nor of any great account; a little man is ready to wish he were as tall as such a one, but he knows it is to no purpose, and therefore does as well as he can with it. Now as we do in reference to our bodily stature, so we should do in reference to our worldly estate. [1.] We should not covet an abundance of the wealth of this world, any more than we would covet the addition of a cubit to one's stature, which is a great deal in a man's height; it is enough to grow by inches; such an addition would but make one unwieldy, and a burden to one's self. [2.] We must reconcile ourselves to our state, as we do to our stature; we must set the conveniences against the inconveniences, and so make a virtue of necessity: what cannot be remedied must be made the best of. We cannot alter the disposals of Providence, and therefore must acquiesce in them, accommodate ourselves to them, and relieve ourselves, as well as we can, against inconveniences, as Zaccheus against the inconvenience of his stature, by climbing into the tree. <div eID="gen21667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21668" type="x-p"/> 4. <hi type="italic">After all these things do the Gentiles seek,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.32">v. 32</reference>. Thoughtfulness about the world is a <hi type="italic">heathenish</hi> sin, and unbecoming <hi type="italic">Christians.</hi> The <hi type="italic">Gentiles</hi> seek <hi type="italic">these things,</hi> because they know not <hi type="italic">better things;</hi> they are eager for this world, because they are strangers to a better; they seek these things with care and anxiety, because they are <hi type="italic">without God in the world,</hi> and understand not his providence. They fear and worship their idols, but know not how to trust them for deliverance and supply, and, therefore, are themselves full of care; but it is a shame for Christians, who build upon nobler principles, and profess a religion which teaches them not only that there is a Providence, but that there are promises made to the good of the life that now is, which teaches them a confidence in God and a contempt of the world, and gives such reasons for both; it is a shame for them to walk as Gentiles walk, and to fill their heads and hearts with these things. <div eID="gen21668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21669" type="x-p"/> 5. <hi type="italic">Your heavenly Father knows ye have need of all these things;</hi> these necessary things, food and raiment; he knows our wants better than we do ourselves; though he be in heaven, and his children on earth, he observes what the least and poorest of them has occasion for (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.9">Rev. ii. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">I know thy poverty.</hi> You think, if such a good friend did not but know your wants and straits, you would soon have relief: your God knows them; and he is your Father that loves you and pities you, and is ready to help you; your heavenly Father, who has wherewithal to supply all your needs: away, therefore, with all disquieting thoughts and cares; go to thy Father; tell him, <hi type="italic">he knows that thou has need of such and such things;</hi> he asks you, <hi type="italic">Children, have you any meat?</hi> <reference osisRef="John.21.5">John xxi. 5</reference>. Tell him whether you have or have not. Though he knows our wants, he will know them from us; and when we have opened them to him, let us cheerfully refer ourselves to his wisdom, power, and goodness, for our supply. Therefore, we should ease ourselves of the burthen of care, by casting it upon God, because it is he <hi type="italic">that careth for us</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.7">1 Pet. v. 7</reference>), and what needs all this ado? If he care, why should be care? <div eID="gen21669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21670" type="x-p"/> 6. <hi type="italic">Seek first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you.</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.33">v. 33</reference>. Here is a double argument against the sin of <hi type="italic">thoughtfulness;</hi> <hi type="italic">take no thought</hi> for your life, the life of the body; for, (1.) You have greater and better things to take thought about, the life of your soul, your eternal happiness; that is the <hi type="italic">one thing needful</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.42">Luke x. 42</reference>), about which you should employ your thoughts, and which is commonly neglected in those hearts wherein worldly cares have the ascendant. If we were but more careful to please God, and to work out our own salvation, we should be less solicitous to please ourselves, and work out an estate in the world. Thoughtfulness for our souls in the most effectual cure of thoughtfulness for the world. (2.) You have a surer and easier, a safer and more compendious way to obtain the necessaries of this life, than by carking, and caring, and fretting about them; and that is, by <hi type="italic">seeking first the kingdom of God,</hi> and making religion your business: say not that this is the way to starve, no, it is the way to be well provided for, even in this world. Observe here, <div eID="gen21670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21671" type="x-p"/> [1.] The great duty required: it is the sum and substance of our whole duty: "<hi type="italic">Seek first the kingdom of God,</hi> mind religion as your great and principle concern." Our duty is to seek; to desire, pursue, and aim at these things; it is a word that has in it much of the constitution of the new covenant in favour of us; <hi type="italic">though we have not attained,</hi> but in many things fail and come short, sincere seeking (a careful concern and an earnest endeavor) is accepted. Now observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The object of this seeking; <hi type="italic">The kingdom of God, and his righteousness;</hi> we must mind heaven as our end, and holiness as our way. "Seek the comforts of the kingdom of grace and glory as your felicity. Aim at the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven;</hi> press towards it; give diligence to make it sure; resolve not to take up short of it; seek for this glory, honour, and immortality; prefer heaven and heavenly blessings far before earth and earthly delights." We make nothing of our religion, if we do not make heaven of it. And with the <hi type="italic">happiness</hi> of this kingdom, seek the <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> of it; <hi type="italic">God's righteousness,</hi> the righteousness which he requires to be wrought <hi type="italic">in</hi> us, and wrought <hi type="italic">by</hi> us, such as exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees; we must <hi type="italic">follow peace and holiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.14">Heb. xii. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The order of it. <hi type="italic">Seek first the kingdom of God.</hi> Let your care for your souls and another world take the place of all other cares: and let all the concerns of this life be made subordinate to those of the life to come: we must seek the things of Christ more than our own things; and if every they come in competition, we must remember to which we are to give the preference. "Seek these things <hi type="italic">first;</hi> first in thy days: let the morning of thy youth be dedicated to God. Wisdom must be sought early; it is good beginning betimes to be religious. Seek the first every day; let waking thoughts be of God." Let this be our principle, to do that first which is most needful, and let him that is the First, have the first. <div eID="gen21671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21672" type="x-p"/> [2.] The gracious promise annexed; <hi type="italic">all these things,</hi> the necessary supports of life, <hi type="italic">shall be added unto you;</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">given over and above;</hi> so it is in the margin. You shall have what you seek, the <hi type="italic">kingdom of God and his righteousness,</hi> for never any sought <hi type="italic">in vain,</hi> that sought <hi type="italic">in earnest;</hi> and besides that, you shall have food and raiment, by way of overplus; as he that buys goods has paper and packthread given him in the bargain. <hi type="italic">Godliness has the promise of the life that now is,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">1 Tim. iv. 8</reference>. Solomon asked wisdom, and had that and other things added to him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.11-2Chr.1.12">2 Chron. i. 11, 12</reference>. O what a blessed change would it make in our hearts and lives, did we but firmly believe this truth, that the best way to be comfortably provided for in this world, is to be most intent upon another world! We then begin at the right end of our work, when we begin with God. If we give diligence to make sure to ourselves the kingdom of God and the righteousness thereof, as to all the things of this life, Jehovah-jireh—the Lord will provide as much of them as he sees good for us, and more we would not wish for. Have we trusted in him for the <hi type="italic">portion of our inheritance</hi> at our end, and shall we not trust him for the <hi type="italic">portion of our cup,</hi> in the way to it? God's Israel were not only brought to Canaan at last, but had their charges borne through the wilderness. O that we were more thoughtful about the things that are not seen, that are eternal, and then the less thoughtful we should be, and the less thoughtful we should need to be, about the things that are seen, that are temporal! <hi type="italic">Also regard not your stuff,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.45.20">Gen. xlv. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.45.23">23</reference>. <div eID="gen21672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21673" type="x-p"/> 7. <hi type="italic">The morrow shall take thought for the things of itself:</hi> <hi type="italic">sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.34">v. 34</reference>. We must not perplex ourselves inordinately about future events, because every day brings along with it its own burthen of cares and grievances, as, if we look about us, and suffer not our fears to betray the succours which grace and reason offer, it brings along with it its own strength and supply too. So that we are here told, <div eID="gen21673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21674" type="x-p"/> (1.) That <hi type="italic">thoughtfulness</hi> for the morrow is <hi type="italic">needless;</hi> <hi type="italic">Let the morrow take thought for the things of itself.</hi> If wants and troubles be renewed with the day, there are aids and provisions renewed likewise; <hi type="italic">compassions,</hi> that are <hi type="italic">new every morning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.3.22-Lam.3.23">Lam. iii. 22, 23</reference>. The saints have a Friend that is <hi type="italic">their arm every morning,</hi> and gives out fresh supplies daily (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.2">Isa. xxxiii. 2</reference>), according <hi type="italic">as the business of every day requires</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.4">Ezra iii. 4</reference>), and so he keeps his people in constant dependence upon him. Let us refer it therefore to the morrow's strength, to do the morrow's work, and bear the morrow's burthen. To-morrow, and the things of it, will be provided for without us; why need we anxiously care for that which is so wisely cared for already? This does not forbid a prudent foresight, and preparation accordingly, but a perplexing solicitude, and a prepossession of difficulties and calamities, which may perhaps never come, or if they do, may be easily borne, and the evil of them guarded against. The meaning is, let us <hi type="italic">mind present duty,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">leave events to God;</hi> do the <hi type="italic">work of the day in its day,</hi> and then let <hi type="italic">to-morrow bring its work along with it.</hi> <div eID="gen21674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21675" type="x-p"/> (2.) That thoughtfulness for the morrow is one of those <hi type="italic">foolish and hurtful lusts,</hi> which those that will be rich fall into, and one of the <hi type="italic">many sorrows,</hi> wherewith they <hi type="italic">pierce themselves through. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.</hi> This present day has trouble enough attending it, we need not <hi type="italic">accumulate</hi> burthens by <hi type="italic">anticipating</hi> our trouble, nor borrow perplexities from to-morrow's evils to add to those of this day. It is uncertain what to-morrow's evils may be, but whatever they be, it is time enough to take thought about them when they come. What a folly it is to take that trouble upon ourselves this day by care and fear, which belongs to another day, and will be never the lighter when it comes? Let us not pull that upon ourselves all together at once, which Providence has wisely ordered to be borne by parcels. The conclusion of this whole matter then is, that it is the will and command of the Lord Jesus, that his disciples should not be their own tormentors, nor make their passage through this world more dark and unpleasant, by their apprehension of troubles, than God has made it by the troubles themselves. By our daily prayers we may procure strength to bear us up under our daily troubles, and to arm us against the temptations that attend them, and then let none of these things move us.  <chapter eID="Matt.6"/> <div eID="gen21675" type="x-p"/>

entries.7ecb3ab8c65473440093d0bee353381dca6052d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13399"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <div sID="gen25530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sermon on the Mount--</hi>continued.<div eID="gen25530" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.6.1-Matt.6.18">Mt 6:1-18</reference>. Further Illustration of the Righteousness of the Kingdom--Its Unostentatiousness.</title> <div sID="gen25531" type="x-p"/> General Caution against Ostentation in Religious Duties (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.1">Mt 6:1</reference>).<div eID="gen25531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25532" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13399"/><hi type="bold">1. Take heed that ye do not your alms--</hi>But the true reading seems clearly to be "your righteousness." The external authority for both readings is pretty nearly equal; but internal evidence is decidedly in favor of "righteousness." The subject of the second verse being "almsgiving" that word--so like the other in Greek--might easily be substituted for it by the copyist: whereas the opposite would not be so likely. But it is still more in favor of "righteousness," that if we so read the first verse, it then becomes a general heading for this whole section of the discourse, inculcating unostentatiousness in all deeds of righteousness--Almsgiving, Prayer, and Fasting being, in that case, but selected examples of this righteousness; whereas, if we read, "Do not your alms," &c., this first verse will have no reference but to that one point. By "righteousness," in this case, we are to understand that same righteousness of the kingdom of heaven, whose leading features--in opposition to traditional perversions of it--it is the great object of this discourse to open up: that righteousness of which the Lord says, "Except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven" (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.20">Mt 5:20</reference>). To "do" this righteousness, was an old and well-understood expression. Thus, "Blessed is he that doeth righteousness at all times" (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.3">Psa 106:3</reference>). It refers to the actings of righteousness in the life--the outgoings of the gracious nature--of which our Lord afterwards said to His disciples, "Herein is My Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be My disciples" (<reference osisRef="John.15.8">Joh 15:8</reference>).<div eID="gen25532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before men, to be seen of them--</hi>with the view or intention of being beheld of them. See the same expression in <reference osisRef="Matt.5.28">Mt 5:28</reference>. True, He had required them to let their light so shine before men that they might see their good works, and glorify their Father which is in heaven (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.16">Mt 5:16</reference>). But this is quite consistent with not making a display of our righteousness for self-glorification. In fact, the doing of the former necessarily implies our not doing the latter.<div eID="gen25533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25534" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven--</hi>When all duty is done to God--as primarily enjoining and finally judging of it--He will take care that it be duly recognized; but when done purely for ostentation, God cannot own it, nor is His judgment of it even thought of--God accepts only what is done to Himself. So much for the general principle. Now follow three illustrations of it.<div eID="gen25534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25535" type="x-p"/> Almsgiving (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.2-Matt.6.4">Mt 6:2-4</reference>). <div eID="gen25535" type="x-p"/>
entries.9559fd9d9f0850e7a7fa0ea55355c022ce96d166: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13400"/><div sID="gen25536" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13400"/><hi type="bold">2. Therefore, when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee--</hi>The expression is to be taken figuratively for blazoning it. Hence our expression to "trumpet."<div eID="gen25536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25537" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the hypocrites do--</hi>This word--of such frequent occurrence in Scripture, signifying primarily "one who acts a part"--denotes one who either pretends to be what he is not (as here), or dissembles what he really is (as in <reference osisRef="Luke.12.1">Lu 12:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2</reference>).<div eID="gen25537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25538" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the synagogues and in the streets--</hi>the places of religious and secular resort.<div eID="gen25538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25539" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they may have glory of men. Verily I say unto you--</hi>In such august expressions, it is the Lawgiver and Judge Himself that we hear speaking to us.<div eID="gen25539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25540" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">They have their reward--</hi>All they wanted was human applause, and they have it--and with it, all they will ever get. <div eID="gen25540" type="x-p"/>
entries.16da1e347774a864f3785bebe6ea387119504bd5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13401"/><div sID="gen25541" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13401"/><hi type="bold">3. But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth--</hi>So far from making a display of it, dwell not on it even in thine own thoughts, lest it minister to spiritual pride. <div eID="gen25541" type="x-p"/>
entries.26e4f33987b9e207fd31a7ca4aef1807f7a99ec0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13402"/><div sID="gen25542" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13402"/><hi type="bold">4. That thine alms may be in secret, and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly--</hi>The word "Himself" appears to be an unauthorized addition to the text, which the sense no doubt suggested. (See <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.25">1Ti 5:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.16">Ro 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">1Co 4:5</reference>).<div eID="gen25542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25543" type="x-p"/> Prayer (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.5">Mt 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen25543" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b9eb090f7aa101fdf86b878a287a356f44d70e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13403"/><div sID="gen25544" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13403"/><hi type="bold">5. And when thou prayest, thou shalt--</hi>or, preferably, "when ye pray ye shall."<div eID="gen25544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not be as the hypocrites are: for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.6.2">Mt 6:2</reference>).<div eID="gen25545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they may be seen of men. Verily I say unto you, They have, &c.--</hi>The standing posture in prayer was the ancient practice, alike in the Jewish and in the early Christian Church. But of course this conspicuous posture opened the way for the ostentatious. <div eID="gen25546" type="x-p"/>
entries.676b32e711e66b59c53f653a3315f92ed0025e29: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13404"/><div sID="gen25547" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13404"/><hi type="bold">6. But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet--</hi>a place of retirement.<div eID="gen25547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly--</hi>Of course, it is not the simple publicity of prayer which is here condemned. It may be offered in any circumstances, however open, if not prompted by the spirit of ostentation, but dictated by the great ends of prayer itself. It is the retiring character of true prayer which is here taught.<div eID="gen25548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25549" type="x-p"/> Supplementary Directions and Model Prayer (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.7-Matt.6.15">Mt 6:7-15</reference>). <div eID="gen25549" type="x-p"/>
entries.09daef4506a38c15d8b6e613f5bc25a47d05ae62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13405"/><div sID="gen25550" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13405"/><hi type="bold">7. But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions--</hi>"Babble not" would be a better rendering, both for the form of the word--which in both languages is intended to imitate the sound--and for the sense, which expresses not so much the repetition of the same words as a senseless multiplication of them; as appears from what follows.<div eID="gen25550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25551" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking--</hi>This method of heathen devotion is still observed by Hindu and Mohammedan devotees. With the Jews, says Lightfoot, it was a maxim, that "Every one who multiplies prayer is heard." In the Church of Rome, not only is it carried to a shameless extent, but, as Tholuck justly observes, the very prayer which our Lord gave as an antidote to vain repetitions is the most abused to this superstitious end; the number of times it is repeated counting for so much more merit. Is not this just that characteristic feature of heathen devotion which our Lord here condemns? But praying much, and using at times the same words, is not here condemned, and has the example of our Lord Himself in its favor. <div eID="gen25551" type="x-p"/>
entries.519d691c9516823d46201095000f28a2a12e147f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13406"/><div sID="gen25552" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13406"/><hi type="bold">8. Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of before ye ask him--</hi>and so needs not to be informed of our wants, any more than to be roused to attend to them by our incessant speaking. What a view of God is here given, in sharp contrast with the gods of the heathen! But let it be carefully noted that it is not as the general Father of mankind that our Lord says, "Your Father" knoweth what ye need before ye ask it; for it is not men, as such, that He is addressing in this discourse, but His own disciples--the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, hungry and thirsty souls, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, who allow themselves to have all manner of evil said against them for the Son of man's sake--in short, the new-born children of God, who, making their Father's interests their own, are here assured that their Father, in return, makes their interests His, and needs neither to be told nor to be reminded of their wants. Yet He will have His children pray to Him, and links all His promised supplies to their petitions for them; thus encouraging us to draw near and keep near to Him, to talk and walk with Him, to open our every case to Him, and assure ourselves that thus asking we shall receive--thus seeking we shall find--thus knocking it shall be opened to us. <div eID="gen25552" type="x-p"/>
entries.944588e5c6a7c2282104086a25a9d034278c912a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13407"/><div sID="gen25553" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13407"/><hi type="bold">9. After this manner--</hi>more simply "Thus."<div eID="gen25553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25554" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore pray ye--</hi>The "ye" is emphatic here, in contrast with the heathen prayers. That this matchless prayer was given not only as a model, but as a form, might be concluded from its very nature. Did it consist only of hints or directions for prayer, it could only be used as a directory; but seeing it is an actual prayer--designed, indeed, to show how much real prayer could be compressed into the fewest words, but still, as a prayer, only the more incomparable for that--it is strange that there should be a doubt whether we ought to pray that very prayer. Surely the words with which it is introduced, in the second utterance and varied form of it which we have in <reference osisRef="Luke.11.2">Lu 11:2</reference>, ought to set this at rest: "When ye pray, say, Our Father." Nevertheless, since the second form of it varies considerably from the first, and since no example of its actual use, or express quotation of its phraseology, occurs in the sequel of the New Testament, we are to guard against a superstitious use of it. How early this began to appear in the church services, and to what extent it was afterwards carried, is known to every one versed in Church History. Nor has the spirit which bred this abuse quite departed from some branches of the Protestant Church, though the opposite and equally condemnable extreme is to be found in other branches of it.<div eID="gen25554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25555" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Model Prayer (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.9-Matt.6.13">Mt 6:9-13</reference>). According to the Latin fathers and the Lutheran Church, the petitions of the Lord's Prayer are seven in number; according to the Greek fathers, the Reformed Church and the Westminster divines, they are only six; the two last being regarded--</hi>we think, less correctly--as one. The first three petitions have to do exclusively with God: "Thy name be hallowed"--"Thy kingdom come"--"Thy will be done." And they occur in a descending scale--from Himself down to the manifestation of Himself in His kingdom; and from His kingdom to the entire subjection of its subjects, or the complete doing of His will. The remaining four petitions have to do with OURSELVES: "Give us our daily bread"--"Forgive us our debts"--"Lead us not into temptation"--"Deliver us from evil." But these latter petitions occur in an ascending scale--from the bodily wants of every day up to our final deliverance from all evil.<div eID="gen25555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25556" type="x-p"/> Invocation:<div eID="gen25556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Our Father which art in heaven--</hi>In the former clause we express His nearness to us; in the latter, His distance from us. (See <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.2">Ec 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.1">Is 66:1</reference>). Holy, loving familiarity suggests the one; awful reverence the other. In calling Him "Father" we express a relationship we have all known and felt surrounding us even from our infancy; but in calling Him our Father "who art in heaven," we contrast Him with the fathers we all have here below, and so raise our souls to that "heaven" where He dwells, and that Majesty and Glory which are there as in their proper home. These first words of the Lord's Prayer--this invocation with which it opens--what a brightness and warmth does it throw over the whole prayer, and into what a serene region does it introduce the praying believer, the child of God, as he thus approaches Him! It is true that the paternal relationship of God to His people is by no means strange to the Old Testament. (See <reference osisRef="Deut.32.6">De 32:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.13">Psa 103:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.16">Is 63:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.4">Jr 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.19">19</reference>; Mal 1:6; 2:10). But these are only glimpses--the "back parts" (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.23">Ex 33:23</reference>), if we may so say, in comparison with the "open face" of our Father revealed in Jesus. (See on <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>). Nor is it too much to say, that the view which our Lord gives, throughout this His very first lengthened discourse, of "our Father in heaven," beggars all that was ever taught, even in God's own Word, or conceived before by His saints, on this subject.<div eID="gen25557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25558" type="x-p"/> First Petition:<div eID="gen25558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25559" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hallowed be--</hi>that is, "Be held in reverence"; regarded and treated as holy.<div eID="gen25559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25560" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy name--</hi>God's name means "Himself as revealed and manifested." Everywhere in Scripture God defines and marks off the faith and love and reverence and obedience He will have from men by the disclosures which He makes to them of what He is; both to shut out false conceptions of Him, and to make all their devotion take the shape and hue of His own teaching. Too much attention cannot be paid to this.<div eID="gen25560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25561" type="x-p"/> Second Petition: <div eID="gen25561" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3156eaffe1f6e88cbe7dd23323cf0509accdc74: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13408"/><div sID="gen25562" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13408"/><hi type="bold">10. Thy kingdom come--</hi>The kingdom of God is that moral and spiritual kingdom which the God of grace is setting up in this fallen world, whose subjects consist of as many as have been brought into hearty subjection to His gracious scepter, and of which His Son Jesus is the glorious Head.
